articles.title: Marcos at Formula 1 race presents opportunities for Philippines, says envoy
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s attendance at the Formula 1 race in Singapore offers opportunities for the Philippines that absent leaders will miss, the Philippine ambassador to…
articles.byline: JONATHAN ANDAL, JEAN MANGALUZ, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 2:22pm

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s attendance at the Formula 1 race in Singapore offers opportunities for the Philippines that absent leaders will miss, the Philippine ambassador to Singapore said on Wednesday.
Ambassador Medardo Macaraig said Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Won had invited Marcos, and the latter won't have to pay for a ticket.
"Halos wala tayo gatsos diyan. Wala siyang babayaran na ticket or kung ano man yung sinasabi… ako rin imbitado ako pero wala rin akong babayaran,” Macaraig said in a press conference in Singapore.
(We spent nearly nothing there. He did not buy a ticket or whatever was being said… I was also invited, and I do not have to pay for anything.)
“Just simply being there already always presents opportunities. Mahirap na mawala tayo doon kasi matatalo tayo sa ibang nandoon," he added.
(It is hard not to be there; we will miss out on opportunities.)
The president is currently in Singapore for a working visit where he is also expected to discuss ASEAN chairship with Wong. Singapore is set to be the 2027 ASEAN Chair.
The Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix events start on Oct. 9 and the main race is scheduled on Oct. 11.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that it was not Marcos’ attendance at the race that should garner attention, but the kind of work he will do in Singapore, especially since he will also attend the Forbes Global CEO Conference.
While Castro did not definitively confirm that Marcos would attend the Formula 1 race, she said that such events would still be important.

“Alam natin na minsan ang mga negosyante, nakakabuo ng magandang rapport, nakakabuo ng magandang pagkakaibigan sa paglalaro ng golf at doon minsan nabubuo ang magagandang kontrata so hindi ibig sabihin kung pupunta man at manonood ang pangulo sa imbitasyon ng gobyerno ng pamahalaan sa F1 Grand Prix, hindi nangahuhulugan na talikuran ang kanyang trabaho sa paghihikayat sa mga investor na mamumuhunan sa bansa,” Castro said.

(We know that sometimes, entrepreneurs make good rapport, good friendships during a game of golf and sometimes, that is there a good contract is formed, so if Marcos does go and attend and watch on behalf of the government’s invitation to the F1 Grand Prix, that does not mean that he is turning his back on his work of encouraging investors to come and invest in the country.)
Marcos has already attended at least two other Formula 1 Singapore races during his presidency. –NB, GMA News

October 7, 2026
Plan for railroad revamp sets goals to 2030

blocks.caption: A new plan sets out a roadmap for development of Germany's railroad systemImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German Transport Ministry has presented a five-year "Infraplan" setting out goals for the improvement of the derelict railroad system.
Transport undersecretary Ulrich Lange said the plan was to be the central compass for the goverment.

"We specify the direction, set priorities and monitor the progress of the implementation," he said as he handed the plan to Philipp Nagl, the chairman of railway operator Deutsche Bahn's infrastructure division, DB InfraGO.
The 160-page plan, which is to be revised each year, covers the period from 2026 to 2030.
The planned renovation measures include repairs, digitization and electrification of routes, reconstruction of stations, noise control and the extension or new construction of lines.
The plan sets out a performance indicator system to make possible a transparent evaluation of the developments in the railroad infrastructure.

There are eight indicators with mandatory targets, such as how many kilometers (miles) of new tracks are laid per year, how many kilometers have been electrified and how many minutes delay are caused by infrastructure defects.
One of the targets set out in the plan is to build 155 kilometers (96 miles) of new track by 2030.
The plan does not, however, contain provisions for financing the railroad renovations, which currently depend on the government budget.
The Transport Ministry is working on a law on a railroad fund that secures financing for several years.
As an example of the problems currently facing train passengers, in September, nearly every second long-distance train was delayed.

articles.title: DILG: Unified 911 system gets 12,000 prank calls daily
articles.summary: Around 12,000 of the 70,000 calls received daily by the country's Unified 911 system are prank calls, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: OUT OF 70K CALLS
Published October 7, 2026 2:00pm
Around 12,000 of the 70,000 calls received daily by the country's Unified 911 system are prank calls, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Wednesday.
Remulla said the prank calls are among the problems affecting the efficiency of the emergency response system.

“Problema namin yung prank calls kasi out of 70,000 calls a day, may mga 12,000 na prank calls. Nakakaantala yun kaya may 6% tayong hindi efficient kasi nakukuha ng oras ng prank calls,” Remulla said in an ambush interview.
(We have a problem with prank calls because out of 70,000 calls a day, there are about 12,000 prank calls. That's why we have 6% that are not efficient because prank calls take up time.)
Despite this, Remulla said the Unified 911 system has an average emergency response time of five to seven minutes.
He said the system has a reported 94% efficiency rate.
Remulla said authorities are working to identify prank callers and remove them from the system to prevent further delays in responding to genuine emergencies.
The DILG chief also said the country's Unified 911 system is drawing interest from other Southeast Asian countries.
According to Remulla, officials from ASEAN countries are visiting the Philippines' 911 center to study how the system operates.
The Unified 911 system is intended to provide a single emergency hotline for police, fire, medical, and other emergency services. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Scientists who put faith in technology less likely to take climate action
articles.summary: ‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are…

blocks.text: Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.

The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

Fabian Dablander, the lead author, said the belief that technology will largely solve climate change and its consequences, labelled “techno-optimism”, can lead to an over reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of the far-reaching socioeconomic transformations needed to address the climate and nature crisis.
“Technological solutions are often politically attractive because they promise to address climate change without requiring changes to how people live and consume,” said Dablander.

“Strikingly, we see the same tendency at the individual level, with greater faith in technological solutions going hand in hand with less engagement in climate action. Yet technology cannot substitute for the broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption that are also needed.”

The study surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries. Overall 27% said they agreed with the statement “technology will largely solve the problems caused by climate change” and 44% disagreed (29% neither agreed nor disagreed).

The “techno-optimist” scientists reported engaging in less civic actions and protests, signed fewer petitions and engaged in less advocacy. They were also less likely to reduce the number of flights they took, cut their car usage or follow a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet.

The report, published in Environmental Research Letters, also found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists with right leaning political views and those working in applied and natural sciences.
after newsletter promotion

Prof Kevin Anderson, one of the world’s leading climate scientists, of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at the University of Manchester, who was not involved in the study, said in his experience “a significant proportion of climate academics who enjoy very high incomes from their work, particularly when those incomes are accompanied by prestige, status and glittering honours, have enthusiastically swallowed the blue pill”.

“It offers a convenient escape from any uncomfortable sense of personal responsibility, allowing them to maintain the comforting fiction that they are deeply concerned about the world their children will inherit while continuing to live lives that contribute disproportionately to the problem.”
He added the “accompanying faith in future technological salvation provides another crutch: a way of postponing difficult choices today by placing hope in solutions that may arrive tomorrow”.

“Yet strikingly often, the evidential basis for these promises falls far short of the standards of scrutiny they would demand of research conducted by others. The result is a remarkable inversion of scientific practice: the more uncomfortable the implications of the evidence, the greater the enthusiasm for believing in a future that the evidence does not support.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Baste Duterte calling out Benny Abante dozing off is AI-generated
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte did not make the remark; it was impeachment court presiding officer Francis ‘Chiz’ Escudero who noticed that Manila 6th District Representative Benny Abante was…

blocks.text: Claim: Video shows Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte throwing shade at Manila 6th District Representative Benny Abante Jr. who was dozing off during Senate impeachment trial.

Why we fact-checked this: The video has already received 130,000 views, 1,100 reactions, 125 shares, and 30 comments as of this posting. It was posted on October 5, days after the mayor attended the impeachment trial as a hostile witness.
Duterte can be seen in the video saying, “May iba sa’tin dito, patulog-tulog lang pero sinusuwelduhan (There are some of us here who just sleep on the job, yet still get paid).”
The video portrays Duterte directly calling out Abante. A clip of the Manila 6th District congressman waking up after the call-out was also attached to the video.
The text on the Facebook reel also reads, “Tulog pa more laki ng sweldo eh nataranta ka atras [Abante] (Keep on sleeping! And yet you earn a huge salary. You panicked, Abante).”

The facts: Duterte did not make the statement. No credible news reports quoted the Davao City mayor making the exact remark. It was the impeachment court presiding officer, Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, who noticed that the congressman was dozing off.

“Before calling on Senator Joel Villanueva, may I ask Congressman Defensor, Congressman Barbers to kindly nudge Cong. Benny a bit? It seems he’s tired. He may want to rest somewhere but at least not right behind the witness,” Escudero said.

The call-out also did not happen while Duterte was on the witness stand. Escudero made the statement while senator-judges were asking Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña.
AI-generated: Reverse image search did not show any credible video similar to the post. It only showed real photos of Duterte in the Senate impeachment trial.

Artificial intelligence (AI) detection tools flagged the video as AI-generated. Hive Moderation detected 66.8% likelihood of being deepfake in the video. Decopy AI flagged the screenshot from the video as 60% likely to be AI-generated. In its analysis, it stated that the photo of Duterte was likely manipulated.

“The image mostly suggests a human origin due to natural skin texture and depth of field, but some minor elements like the flat clothing texture and expression rigidity could hint at subtle AI enhancement or smoothing,” it stated.

Duterte: The Davao City mayor appeared before the Senate impeachment court on September 29 as a hostile witness. He was asked about the contracts of the Davao City government with Gencorp, which is linked to the Vice President. Duterte maintained that he had no involvement in the contracts with the company.
Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar AI-generated videos about public officials:

blocks.text: A Queensland man has been charged with the murder of his three-month-old baby son, after the boy died in hospital this week.
The infant, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with “significant internal injuries”. The boy had been on life support.
Uneeb Ullah, 28, was arrested on Tuesday evening and charged with the boy’s murder, which is designated a domestic violence offence.
His matter was mentioned briefly in court on Wednesday but Ullah was not required to appear and did not enter a plea.

Police said detectives from the Child Protection Investigation Unit launched an investigation on 1 October after the boy was taken to Ipswich hospital with significant injuries, and that the nature of those injuries prompted hospital staff to report the matter to police.
He was later transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, DI Michael Manago said the mother of the child was “extremely upset” and that both parents, who were born overseas, have limited support.
The boy was the couple’s only child.
“This is a terribly tragic event involving a very vulnerable young member of the community,” Det Insp. Manago said.
“The boy’s mother is extremely upset as you can imagine; this is a terribly tragic event.
“She is struggling, but we’re offering her all the support that we can through this very difficult time.”
Police said they had spoken to the couple several times since they opened the investigation. The investigation would include looking at the “nature and dynamics” of the boy’s parents’ relationship.
“It’s an incredibly confronting and difficult investigation,” Manago said.
“We were conducting our investigation throughout the last number of days and gathering evidence.
after newsletter promotion
When Ullah’s case came before the court on Wednesday, police prosecutor Ben Messina asked it be stood down until later in the day.

“I received a phone call this morning … that potentially more material would be provided and asked [that] this matter be stood down to the end of the list,” Messina said of the “relatively vague request”.
The magistrate agreed to re-mention the case if other charges were laid.
Kirstyn Nicholson, a Legal Aid solicitor representing Ullah, did not apply for bail and sought an adjournment.
Ullah was remanded in custody until the matter returns to court on 26 October.

articles.title: Flydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinised
articles.summary: Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne New Zealand authorities have launched their own…
articles.byline: Eva Corlett in Auckland and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne

blocks.text: New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

Hammami, an Omani national, had allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect he originally planned for such an attack in July, but postponed it.
The New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.
“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statement
The police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.
New Zealand joins multiple countries scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree, RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.
On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.

The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.
On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.

“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.
“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

articles.title: Leandro Leviste must first subject himself to court to post bail -- DOJ spox
articles.summary: Justice spokesperson Polo Martinez on Wednesday said Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste must first subject himself to the court before he can post bail.

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 1:16pm
Justice spokesperson Polo Martinez on Wednesday said Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste must first subject himself to the court before he can post bail.
This comes following the Makati court’s issuance of an arrest warrant against Leviste over an alleged violation of the Public Service Act.
“As a general rule, an accused must first submit to the jurisdiction of the court, either through arrest or voluntary surrender, before bail may be granted,” Martinez told reporters.
“Thus, if the accused is abroad, he would have to submit himself to the jurisdiction of the court before he may avail himself of bail,” he added.
According to the Department of Justice, bail is fixed at P72,000.
Leviste is in France taking care of his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, who is on medical leave, his spokesperson said last September 25.
Meanwhile, Martinez said it is too early to say whether any action will be taken regarding Leviste’s passport.

“Under the New Philippine Passport Act, there are specific grounds for the cancellation of a passport, including when the holder has been convicted of a criminal offense or has been declared a fugitive from justice, in both cases upon order of the court,” he said.
“Neither circumstance is present at this time,” he added.

The DOJ said the case stemmed from a finding of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction that SPSBC willfully neglected and intentionally failed to comply with its obligations under its legislative franchise.
Leviste earlier said the Energy Department's allegations against him are baseless and a threat to public entities, including media organizations.
“The only complaint I’ve seen is from the media, and based on that, I can say: super duper hina,” Leviste said. (The complaint is very weak.)
Leviste said the DOE suit sets a precedent for future administrations to file nuisance complaints against officers and directors of public utilities in the Philippines. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has launched a celebratory campaign — dubbed 'Seva Sankalp' — to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 25 years as head of a government.
On October 7, 2001, Modi was first sworn in as chief minister of the western state of Gujarat.

"As the head of the government, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi's twenty-five years are a testament to service, dedication, good governance, and strong willpower," India's Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said in a post on X.
Several politicians from the BJP echoed his sentiments, contratulating the premier on his service.

At the center of today's festivities is a bike rally. News agency ANI reported that participants loaded up on bikes arrived in the northern holy city of Varanasi from a different holy city of Tirupati in southern India.

"Covering 2000 km (1,242 miles) after visiting the Balaji temple in Andhra Pradesh, a team of 40 youths—who are also party office-bearers—undertook a journey," a local minister from the state of Uttar Pradesh said, adding that a temple would soon be built to mark the occasion.
Several states BJP-ruled states are organizing public gatherings where speeches by Modi and BJP party President Nitin Nabin would be telecast on giant screens.

The celebrations are reminiscent of another recent campaign for Modi's birthday on September 17. Critics had then pointed out that the government was spending massively on public relations, advertising and celebrations, while advising Indians to practice austerity to counter the fallout from global conflicts.

articles.title: Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild
articles.summary: Three years on from the attack on Nir Oz, in which 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage, some survivors have returned to live there.

blocks.text: Dalit Ram Aharon and her husband Achi say they want to move back to Nir Oz "in the memory" of the friends they lost in the 7 October attacks
ByYolande Knell
Middle East CorrespondentReporting fromKibbutz Nir Oz

Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.
"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.
By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.

The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."

As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.

Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.
The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A red sticker on a postbox indicates those who were killed in the Hamas attacks; black indicates those who were taken hostage

blocks.text: A red sticker on a postbox indicates those who were killed in the Hamas attacks; black indicates those who were taken hostage
Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.

"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.
"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."
An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.
Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.

Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.

blocks.caption: Map of Nir Oz.

blocks.text: As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.

The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."

The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.

The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.

On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.

Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.
Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.

"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dalit says Shiri Bibas, who was killed along with her two children after being taken hostage, was "like a sister"

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy of Dalit Ram Aharon
Dalit says Shiri Bibas, who was killed along with her two children after being taken hostage, was "like a sister"
"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."
While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.

Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.
Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.

They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.

"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.
However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.

"Terrorists penetrated 97% of the households and burned down almost 50%," says Emi Palmor, director of the rebuilding project. "Now it's the only place in Israel that has to be completely demolished and completely replanned."
She says that it is a difficult balance to redesign the kibbutz so that it feels like home but does not cause new trauma to those who return.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Emi Palmor is the director of the Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Project at Nir Oz

blocks.text: Emi Palmor is the director of the Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Project at Nir Oz

"It's a huge debate – a very painful debate," Emi says. "Some people say, 'If I come back here, I want the entire area to look serene. I don't have to be reminded because I remember every day the people I lost.' Other people say, 'There is such denial – if we will take down the last houses, who will ever believe?'"
About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage after an estimated 6,000 Palestinians streamed across the Gaza border during the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN.

Despite the US-brokered ceasefire deal which brought the last hostages home a year ago, violence has continued, including near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced and much of the territory is in ruins. US President Donald Trump's peace plan is at an impasse.

For Israelis, there are outstanding questions over accountability for the failure of Israel's security forces to have prevented the 7 October attacks. People from Nir Oz favour a comprehensive state commission of inquiry and still have major security concerns.

Survivors, including the Aharons, suffer from post-traumatic stress. Dalit recalls how her eldest son, Uri, turned nine on 7 October 2023 - when they spent the day hiding in their bomb shelter. "He told me, 'Mum, I don't want to die on my birthday,'" she says. "You know people don't understand that we still live this horrible day."
This anniversary of the attacks is the first with no hostages remaining in Gaza. "It's a very big relief," Dalit says. Achi sees that now is the time to focus on personal healing.

"Until the hostages came back, it was the only thing on our mind," he says. "Now you have the time to concentrate on yourself, on what you lost, what you need. Now it's our recovery or some kind of recovery as much as we can."

articles.title: Tories delight as satirical tapestry pokes fun at ‘turncoat’ Robert Jenrick
articles.summary: Reminders of banished Reform UK defector were all around the Conservative party conference in Birmingham As Kemi Badenoch basked in the applause of the Tory faithful at the close of her pivotal…

blocks.text: As Kemi Badenoch basked in the applause of the Tory faithful at the close of her pivotal speech at Conservative party conference last year, one member of her shadow cabinet looked less than enthused.

Robert Jenrick, bested by Badenoch in the leadership contest a year earlier, looked on, and – as one shadow cabinet member now recalls – had to be prodded by Lord Ashcroft to applaud. “If you’re plotting against someone, then you at least pretend to like them,” they say. “The thing about Robert is he’s not even a good machiavellian.”

Jenrick left the party a matter of months later, swiftly – and publicly – ejected by an ice-cold Badenoch after she got wind that he was planning to defect to Reform. This week, as the Conservative ranks enjoy their annual knees-up in Birmingham, the now Reform UK economy spokesperson has been swiping from the sidelines, accusing his old party of “once again copying our policies”.

But while Jenrick’s physical presence may be absent from the migraine-inducing interior of the International Convention Centre in the West Midlands, members could be forgiven for sighing that everywhere they looked, something reminded them of him.

At the heart of the conference, members queue to chortle at depictions of Jenrick in the Conservatives’ own “Birmingham tapestry”, a 27-metre (88ft) woven graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics, as seen through Conservative eyes.

Featuring Badenoch as a glorious 11th-century conquering warrior, the “tapestry” also depicts a tiny Jenrick wailing as he loses the leadership contest, as he watches a crowd cheering on his victor. A little later, under the heading “Expelleth the Turncoat”, an outsized Badenoch is seen banishing her tiny, sobbing former colleague – as she stands next to a photocopier where, legend has it, Jenrick’s resignation letter was found.

“I think it’s great fun; every story needs a villain and he’s ours,” says one party member who’d travelled from Scotland for the event. “He’s not a big figure here any more, he’s just a figure of fun.”

Another member says they voted for Jenrick in the leadership election and had felt let down by his plots to remove the leader after failing to get the top job. “The way he did what he did was spiteful, petty and childish. I was a massive fan, but now I couldn’t care less what he does,” he says. Referring to Jenrick’s hyperactive social media output, which regularly show the Reform economy spokesperson confronting fare-dodgers and shoplifters, he rolls his eyes. “It’s just attention-seeking, isn’t it?” he says. “I do wonder now, though, as Reform falter, if he regrets what he did. I hope so.”

The schadenfreude at Jenrick’s fading star is palpable at this conference. Unprompted, shadow cabinet ministers bring him up with unbridled delight. “I miss him like I would miss an abscess in my molar,” remarks one senior Tory, before wondering aloud about whether Jenrick was likely to be punched in the face during one of his vigilante operations.

Others are surprised at their own strength of feeling towards a former colleague. “Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left the party,” says one senior member. Repeating the mantra that they are more united behind Badenoch than any other leader in years, some credit Jenrick for bringing them closer together, because he had “briefed against everybody”. Another adds: “Rob leaving was like pulling out a splinter.”

The commentary is not limited to gossip around the bars of Birmingham’s Hyatt hotel. Mentions of Jenrick are met with groans in the audience at a packed fringe event of shadow cabinet ministers hosted by More in Common. Asked if he would consider taking Jenrick or any of the other three Tory MPs who defected back, the response of Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, is unequivocal. “No, no, no and no,” he says. Was he relieved they were gone? “Yes, yes, yes and yes.”

Badenoch has made clear that neither Jenrick nor his fellow defectors (variously described by her team as “venal”, “mad” and “hopeless”) would ever be welcome back, going as far as thanking Nigel Farage for doing the “spring cleaning” of her party for her.

Others suggest Reform were welcome to one of their former star players. “Good luck to his new friends in Reform,” one says. “It’s all about Rob and his own ambitions and he’d elbow them into the path of an oncoming express train if it meant he got ahead.”

Appreciating the Birmingham tapestry in between panel sessions, the shadow undersecretary for environment, food and rural affairs, Aphra Brandreth, insists the party is completely over Jenrick, although his shadow here suggests there may still be some healing left to do. “Honestly I don’t spend any time thinking about Robert Jenrick,” she says, with a benevolent smile. “He’s gone, and we’ve all moved on.”

articles.title: O2 signs record £200m deal to keep London venue’s naming rights
articles.summary: Exclusive: 10-year sponsorship extension at a 50% premium on last agreement crowns bonanza year for live venue O2 has struck a record £200m deal to retain the naming rights to the London venue the O2…

blocks.text: O2 has struck a record £200m deal to retain the naming rights to the London venue the O2 in what is thought to be the largest renewal of its kind in UK history.

The 10-year agreement will extend O2’s relationship until at least 2038. It cements the sponsorship as the second longest-running UK stadium naming rights deal after Arsenal’s partnership for the football club’s London ground,

Under the deal with Anschutz Entertainment Group (AEG), which bought the site of the ill-fated Millennium Dome five years after it was shut following the millennium celebrations, O2 is thought to be paying about £20m a year in the wide-ranging partnership.

This is an almost 50% increase on the annual amount under the existing deal which was due to expire at the end of next year. It is more than triple the £6m a year O2 paid in its initial 10-year deal when the future success of the O2 and surrounding site was far from certain.

blocks.caption: Virgin Media O2’s Gareth Griffiths (left) and AEG’s Paul Samuels at the O2 in London. Photograph: Doug Peters/PA

blocks.text: “Everyone thought it would never work, that it was crazy building on the site of the Millennium Dome, it was considered the biggest white elephant,” said Paul Samuels, president of global partnerships at AEG International, talking to the Guardian.
“In the first deal we were talking about whether to put in clauses if the O2 couldn’t hit 100 shows a year – last year we did 239. We opened in June 2007 with Bon Jovi and the rest is history.”

Newly published accounts show that the O2 enjoyed the best year in its 19-year history in 2025. Pre-tax profits surged 18% to £76.5m, while revenues climbed 14% to £148.6m, as music fans put aside cost-of-living concerns to see acts including Lady Gaga, Katy Perry, Radiohead and Usher.
The record year resulted in a healthy £27.5m dividend being paid to its US parent company.

“People will opt to save money on other things but still want to go out and spend money on live entertainment,” said Samuels. “And when it comes to technological change like AI, it can change the world but it won’t change the desire for a live experience, like music and sport.”
Samuels said that each time the sponsorship deal nears renewal he receives a lot of interest from brands hoping to take over the naming rights.

However, Gareth Griffiths, director of partnerships and sponsorships at themobile operator’s parent company Virgin Media O2, said the deal had worked so well that it was agreed within an exclusivity period.
A key component of the deal is a 50% increase in the number of priority tickets made available to O2 customers, granting access to tickets to events 48 hours before they go on general sale.
O2 sells more than 1.7m tickets each year through its Priority Tickets programme across the 20 music venues it sponsors in the UK.
after newsletter promotion
“The O2 has been an amazing brand asset for us,” said Griffiths. “Two-and-a-half million people come to the [main] arena each year, and 7.5 million come to everything else that is on offer.
“Music is right in the core DNA of our brand. Customer retention is absolutely crucial and driving loyalty through entertainment is a sweet spot for the business.”
Last year, O2 lost more than 100,000 customers after a backlash following the introduction of hefty price rises.
Last month, it was reported that VMO2’s joint owners – Liberty Global and Telefonica – want to cut £600m in costs to calm investor fears over a £22bn debt pile.
“Every pound we spend we do so very carefully,” said Griffiths. “This has been such a big success for the brand.
“Churn is still one of the most important metrics in the business, it is about keeping hold of valuable customers. Both of our shareholders are absolutely fully committed to this.
“This is a 10-year investment in the UK … a huge sign of intent. It has long been proven that growth comes from investment in your brand.”

articles.title: Wanted: children to rear harvest mice at home for wild release in Devon
articles.summary: Teenagers Eva Wishart and Emily Smith launch project to breed and release 250 of the tiny animals by September Children in Devon are being invited to become “citizen captive breeders”, rearing…

blocks.text: Children in Devon are being invited to become “citizen captive breeders”, rearing harvest mice at home for release into the wild to help revive endangered nature.
Wild Pets, a new conservation project launched by two 14-year-old friends, is seeking 20 Devon-based children to rear hundreds of mice after the duo’s own successful restoration efforts.

Eva Wishart and Emily Smith bred several hundred harvest mice in tanks in their garages and released them on a nature reserve in Devon, south-west England, where the mice have begun breeding in the wild again.

The tiny harvest mouse, the UK’s smallest native rodent, is the only British mammal to have a prehensile tail, which can grasp or hold objects. It uses its tail to clamber up grass stems, which were once commonplace in fields, meadows and scrubland but have become far more scarce because of agricultural intensification.

blocks.caption: A harvest mouse at Perivale Wood nature reserve in west London in 2024. Photograph: David Parry/PA Media Assignments/PA

blocks.text: Eva founded Wild Pets after feeling sorry for traditional pets such as hamsters and goldfish that are confined to cages and small spaces, while also worrying about the extinction crisis and ecological collapse. She began breeding harvest mice aged 10.

“I took them to school once to do a talk when I was 10,” she said. “It was the most popular I’ve ever been and everyone voted that we should keep them. So then we kept them in school in a big tank in the corner for six weeks. It was great. They had loads of babies.”
In 2025 her Wild Pets project was a runner-up in Prince William’s junior Earthshot competition, with crowdfunding supporting the first harvest mouse release.

Advised by the ecologist and rewilder Derek Gow, who has managed long-running captive-breeding programmes for water voles, beavers, storks and other mammals and birds, Eva and Emily last year released hundreds of captive-bred mice into a nature reserve.

blocks.caption: ‘Eva and Emily last year released hundreds of captive-bred mice into a nature reserve’: harvest mice are released in Tiverton, Devon, in 2025. Photograph: Karen Robinson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The new population survived and maternal nests – distinctive grass balls expertly woven and suspended in tussocky grassland or scrub by the females – were found on the reserve this year. Chris Packham called the Wild Pets concept “truly sensational” on BBC’s Springwatch.

The expanded project, supported by Gow, the Devon Environment Foundation, Mid Devon district council and the Naturesave Trust, is seeking applications from children aged eight to 13, who can apply via the Wild Pets website.

Eva said young wild breeders would require a certain sense of “responsibility but most of all, really, enthusiasm, because if you’re really enthusiastic and passionate about something, with a bit of help, you’ll probably do it. Mainly we’re just looking for passionate kids.”

Wild Pets will provide a pair of harvest mice and all the equipment after a training day next spring at Gow’s Rewilding Coombeshead centre in Devon. The children will breed the mice, which can have multiple litters over the summer, with the aim of releasing 250 next September.
after newsletter promotion

Emily said taking even modest action to help wildlife alleviated feelings of anxiety about environmental destruction. “It definitely makes you feel a lot better in the long run. It just makes you feel like you’re actually doing something rather than just watching it all happen,” she said.

Eva added: “Everything’s really scary at the moment for our future, on the news and at school. Everything’s very dark. So doing something, even if it’s only a tiny thing in a tiny corner of Devon, helps us feel a bit better.”

Packham said: “It’s so inspirational when young people think of an idea and then make it happen. It’s so, so important. What I like about young people doing things is that they think clearly, speak clearly and they get things done. Top work Eva and Emily. This is a really brilliant, brilliant project.”

The founders of Wild Pets hope to expand the wild breeding programmes to other small native species that should be more commonplace in Britain such as common lizards, stag beetles, mole crickets and glowworms.
Eva said: “In the first year we’re just inspiring 20 kids, but then, next year, we’re going to inspire the whole country to become conservationists and care about the natural world.”

articles.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
articles.summary: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.

blocks.text: As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.
"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.
"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.
That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.
He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.
"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.
If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.
"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.
Top picture credit: BBC / Getty Images

articles.title: Who are the bank representatives testifying on Day 35 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial?
articles.summary: Several bank representatives took the witness stand on Wednesday, October 7, to testify in the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 12:53pm
Several bank representatives took the witness stand on Wednesday, October 7, to testify in the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.
During the 35th day of the trial, the House prosecution panel first called to the stand Arcy James Gonzales, the branch manager of Asia United Bank (AUB) Davao Toril Branch.
“Primary function ko po is oversight ng transaction records… I’m running the branch. Oversight ng mga records and documents, transactions mga ganon,” he said.
(My primary functions are oversight of transaction records… I’m running the branch. Oversight of records and documents, transactions, things like that.)
Gonzales said he was a part of the branch since early 2023.
After him, the House prosecution panel called on Irene Joy Ishida, the head of Branch Operations Department of the Philippine Savings Bank (PSB).

“My department supervises the operations of the branches of PSB. As part of my functions as the department head, I ensure that branches are able to strictly adhere to the policies, the internal controls, the regulatory requirements, and the standards set by the PS Bank,” she said.
Niña Feren Aguilar, the head of the Anti-Money Laundering Division of the Metropolitan Bank and Trust Company (Metrobank), then testified after Ishida.
Aguilar said she oversees the bank’s compliance to the Anti-Money Laundering Act.
“As the head of the Anti-Money Laundering Division, I have access to all the records for the accounts subject of the subpoena,” she said.
She said she has been head of the division for over a year.
The House prosecution panel also called on as a witness Leslie Cham, the Branch Banking Group head of the Security Bank Corporation (SBC).
“I actually supervise the overall, the branch banking of the bank with regards to the distribution channel. So we are handling sales and service,” Cham said.
He said he has been working in the position for 18 years.
Prior to SBC, he said he worked for City Trust Bank, the PCI Bank, the Standard Chartered Bank, and the China Trust Banking Corporation.

Duterte is the subject of an impeachment trial, where she is accused of committing grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and others, misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and bribery. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Henry Aguda remains as DICT secretary --Palace
articles.summary: Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda will stay on as the agency"s chief, according to Palace Press Officer Claire Castro on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 12:52pm
Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda will stay on as the agency’s chief, according to Palace Press Officer Claire Castro on Wednesday.
In a video report from Jonathan Andal, Castro addressed rumors that Aguda has resigned.
Citing Presidential Communications Office Secretary Dave Gomez, Castro said that the Palace has received no such information. She also read a statement from Aguda.

“I am aware of the reports circulating regarding my position as Secretary of the Department of Information and Communications Technology. At this time, I remain focused on carrying out my responsibilities and ensuring the continuity of the Department’s work,” Aguda said in his statement.

“As Secretary of DICT, I serve at the pleasure of the President, and I fully recognize and respect the President’s prerogative in matters concerning his Cabinet and his administration. My focus remains on carrying out my responsibilities and serving the Filipino people to the best of my ability,” he added.
Aguda began his stint as the DICT secretary in March 2025, replacing Ivan Uy.

Rumors of Aguda’s resignation came amid the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center’s controversial decision to ban Discord following a series of school shootings. The agency cited the platform’s non-cooperation with Philippine authorities to establish a local office in the country. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Former bishop sentenced to more than six years in prison for sexually abusing young Aboriginal men
articles.summary: Christopher Alan Saunders becomes highest-ranked Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse over his time as member of clergy A former high-ranking Catholic known for hosting boozy parties will…

blocks.text: A former high-ranking Catholic known for hosting boozy parties will spend at least four and a half years behind bars for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men.
The ex-bishop of Broome Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 sex offences after a jury trial in the West Australian district court.
The offending between 2008 and 2019 included one count of sexual penetration without consent and a dozen unlawful and indecent assault charges.
Saunders was sentenced on Wednesday to six years and six months’ imprisonment.
He will be eligible for parole after serving four years and six months.
Unless acquitted on appeal, the long-serving bishop would be the highest-ranking Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse over his time as a member of the clergy.
The late Cardinal George Pell was found guilty in 2018 but later acquitted by the high court of raping one choirboy and molesting another in 1996.
Saunders was acquitted by the jury of six other charges, including two counts of indecently dealing with a child over 16 under his authority and four counts of unlawful and indecent assault.
He was acquitted of a further seven similar charges during the trial due to the lack of evidence.
The sentence was backdated to August when Saunders was convicted and taken into custody.

Prosecutors said Saunders, known as Brother B by his victims, put on alcohol-fuelled parties at Catholic church-owned properties to get access to Aboriginal boys and men so he could sexually assault them.
“The accused had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men and a tendency to act on that interest when the opportunity presented itself,” the prosecutor, Adam Ebell, previously told the court.
Saunders was ordained as the second Broome bishop in 1996 and presided over 13 schools and nine parishes before stepping aside in 2020 when the sex abuse claims became public.
after newsletter promotion
Pope Francis accepted his resignation a year later.
A church probe into the retired clergyman’s activities was suspended when the West Australian police started investigating him.
It will restart now the trial has finished.
“Its findings will inform decisions in Rome about Christopher Saunders’ position in the church,” archbishop Timothy Costelloe said in August.
Costelloe said the jury’s guilty verdict concerned crimes “that violate the dignity and betray the trust of victims and survivors”.
“The victims, survivors and other witnesses who came forward showed great courage and resilience throughout a long and difficult process,” he said.

articles.title: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze
articles.summary: Russian officials said a Liberian-flagged tanker was attacked and a crew of 23 Indian nationals rescued An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire…

blocks.text: An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.
The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.
“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.
A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.
Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.

Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.
Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.

blocks.caption: Russia says a tanker has caught fire in the Black Sea

blocks.text: Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels were had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.

Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.

After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.” Radev said after an emergency government meeting.
Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km kilometers) off Bulgaria ’s coast, he said.
Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.
Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko said ‌on Telegram.
Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.
A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged ⁠an industrial facility, ​officials said, without giving details.

Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Firm linked to Sara Duterte's husband closed two bank accounts in July --witness
articles.summary: The two checking accounts of Cale88, one of the listed business interest of Vice President Sara"s husband, Manases Carpio, were closed last July, the same month that the Vice President Sara Duterte"s…

blocks.text: AS IMPEACHMENT TRIAL BEGAN
Published October 7, 2026 12:38pm

The two checking accounts of Cale88, one of the listed business interest of Vice President Sara’s husband, Manases Carpio, were closed last July, the same month that the Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial started.
Leslie Cham, the Security Bank Branch Banking Group head, made the testimony during Day 35 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President during the questioning of Senator judge Francis Pangilinan.
Cham testified that two checking accounts of Cale88 Foods Corporation were opened in August 2024 and October 2025, respectively, but both were closed in July 2026.
"Both closed on July 2026," Cham said.
The impeachment trial of the Vice President started on July 6.
Cham said that one of the accounts' ending balance as of the end of 2025 is at least P332,000, while the other account posted an ending balance of P21,000 as of December 2025.

The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura earlier testified that Cale88 Foods Corporation had aggregate covered suspicious transactions amounting to P1.25 billion from 2022 to 2025.
“We have CTRs (Covered Transaction Reports), STRs (Suspicious Transaction Reports) from 2022 to 2025. For Cale88, the aggregated amount is P1,254,736,297.08,” Buenaventura said.
Buenaventura also told the Senate court that the P1.25 billion in covered and suspicious transactions include the P319 million inward remittance from China that Cale 88 received.

Cale88 is one of the business interests listed under the joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) of the Vice President and her husband in multiple years, including the years when the Vice President already assumed office.
Duterte’s defense team maintained that an STR is not a sufficient basis to conclude that the Vice President engaged in illegal transactions.
They also said that the witness affirmed this, stating that it is a legal requirement and that no illegality can be concluded solely on the basis of the report. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Where is Spain headed after the snap election announcement?
articles.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is taking a gamble by calling an early election in Spain. The housing crisis, migration and the rise of the right-wing populist Vox party are all likely to dominate the…

image.caption: Early on Monday morning, Prime Minister Sanchez announced snap parliamentary electionsImage: LA MONCLOA/AFP

blocks.text: Spain's economic data has been positive recently, but politically, the country has been mired in a prolonged crisis for months.
On Monday, the social democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded with a surprise move to break the deadlock: He is calling an early election for November 29.
Why is Sanchez calling an election now?

The sudden announcement followed a dramatic political defeat for the government. On Friday, October 2, Sanchez's emergency measures to tackle the housing crisis failed in parliament. Seven lawmakers from the conservative Catalan separatist party Junts, whose support the government has relied on since 2023, brought the measures down. Sanchez says he is now calling for a "much broader progressive majority."

blocks.caption: Set to profit from the snap election: Vox leader Santiago AbascalImage: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: The defeat came after months of growing instability in the government's parliamentary base. Spain's parliament has not passed a regular budget since 2023.

The recent crisis over mass migration to Ceuta and several corruption scandals involving allegations against the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and people close to Sanchez have piled pressure onto the government.
And then came Maricarmen. The forced eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal last month suddenly turned the housing shortage into the headline political issue.
The fact that his emergency measures were rejected in parliament allows Sanchez to position himself as a defender of tenants. However, it remains to be seen whether that strategy will pay off.
What role is pressure from the street protests playing?

The housing shortage has been at the top of Spaniards' list of concerns for around three years. According to estimates by the Bank of Spain, the country is currently short of around 750,000 homes, and the figure could exceed one million by 2028.

More than half of 18- to 34-year-olds live with their parents or depend on them financially. Property prices have recently been rising three times as fast as wages. In Spain, social housing accounts for just around 1.7 percent of the country's housing stock, putting it at the lower end of the EU scale in comparison with other member states.
Housing crisis triggers snap election in Spain

It is hardly surprising, then, that protest camps sprang up in Madrid and elsewhere in response to the plight of Maricarmen Abascal, and tens of thousands took to the streets across the country. After the government's measures were rejected, the trade unions CCOO and UGT even announced a 24-hour general strike.

These dividing lines, however, do not simply split the government and the opposition. The tenants' movement also views Sanchez's plans as insufficient. The conservative opposition People's Party (PP) and parts of the business community, meanwhile, warn that tighter rent controls could make the problem worse.
Is Sanchez's model of governance coming to an end?

Since the 2023 election, Pedro Sanchez has governed without a majority in parliament. His social democratic PSOE formed a coalition with the left-wing Sumar alliance, but also depended on the support of smaller parties. These included Basque and Catalan regional parties, but above all the Catalan separatists of Junts.

That meant its seven lawmakers were repeatedly able to determine whether government legislation secured a majority or not. Over the course of the parliamentary term, this arrangement became increasingly unstable. In the first half of 2026 alone, the government lost almost one in four votes.

blocks.caption: For three years, the government has failed to get a budget through parliamentImage: Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Evidence of the extent of this political deadlock is the state budget: Spain continues to work with the 2023 budget because the prime minister has been unable to get a new budget through parliament in his entire term. Junts ultimately refused to support Sanchez on housing policy, leaving him without backing on an issue that has been at the top of the political agenda following nationwide protests.
What was the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis?

At the end of July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta within a short period of time. Although the government declared the crisis over soon afterward, at least 10,000 migrants were still in the exclave two months later, which has a population of only around 80,000. It was not until last Sunday that police cleared an improvised camp where around 3,000 people had been living.
Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing

The crisis altered Sanchez's previously relatively liberal migration policy. A new draft seen by Reuters proposes accelerated asylum procedures and deportations, as well as tighter rules. Human rights organizations have voiced sharp criticism.
How strong is the opposition?
At first glance, Spain's conservative PP is entering the snap parliamentary election at the end of November as the frontrunner to become the largest parliamentary group.

The real winner of recent months, however, is the right-wing populist Vox party. It is now polling at just over 18%, around six percentage points more than in the 2023 election. A strong Vox turnout could increase PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo's chances of gathering enough seats for a governing majority from parties right of center.

blocks.caption: The man hoping to become Spain's next prime minister: PP leader Alberto Nunez FeijooImage: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Vox leader Santiago Abascal is now confidently setting conditions for cooperation. Priority for Spanish citizens, economic deregulation and a significantly tougher migration policy, including the far-right concept of deporting foreign nationals to their countries of origin.

For his part, Feijoo faces a difficult balancing act. To replace Sanchez, he also needs to win voters from the political center. At the same time, he may need a partner for a governing majority who is steering the campaign significantly further to the right.
Will Spain also be voting on Trump and Europe's political direction?

In international media coverage, Sanchez is repeatedly portrayed as Europe's most prominent critic of Donald Trump. The prime minister rejected the US president's demand for defense spending to rise to 5% of GDP, refused to allow US bases in Spain to be used for the war against Iran and criticized US-Israeli attacks.

As a result, Trump even threatened at one point to cut off trade relations. At the same time, Sanchez explicitly contrasts his more liberal migration policy with Trump's deportation policies and attacks what he calls the "tech oligarchs" from the United States.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez (left) has positioned himself as a strong European voice against Donald TrumpImage: Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sanchez is also one of the most prominent social democratic leaders of a major EU country. If the left were to lose the upcoming Spanish election, the European Council would lose one of its most outspoken voices against Donald Trump . It would also lose a prime minister who has opposed climbing defense spending, defended a more liberal approach to migration and criticized Israel more sharply over the war in Gaza than most of his European counterparts.
This article originally appeared in German.

articles.title: Leandro Leviste on arrest warrant: 'Don't worry about me'
articles.summary: Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste on Wednesday told his supporters not to worry about him following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him over an alleged violation of the Public…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 12:19pm

Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste on Wednesday told his supporters not to worry about him following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him over an alleged violation of the Public Service Act (PSA).
“Salamat sa lahat ng sumusuporta. Huwag niyo akong alalahanin, maliit na bagay lang ito kumpara sa ibang nangyayari,” Leviste said in a statement.
(Thank you to everyone who has been supporting me. Don’t worry about me, this is just a small matter compared to what is happening elsewhere.)
“Kayo ang inaalala ko (You are the ones I’m worried about),” he added. He did not elaborate.

On Monday, a Makati Regional Trial Court (RTC) issued the warrant against Leviste over an alleged violation of Section 25 of Commonwealth Act No. 146, as amended by Republic Act No. 11659, or the PSA. Bail was set at P72,000.
The case stemmed from a complaint filed by the Department of Energy (DOE) with the Department of Justice in May against Leviste and five officials of Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation (SPBC).

The DOE alleged that the company failed to construct and provide electric power to customers and end users in remote, unviable, unserved, or underserved areas, as required under its 2019 legislative franchise granted through Republic Act No. 11357.
Leviste is currently in France, where he has been taking care of his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, who is on medical leave, according to their spokesperson, lawyer Tony La Viña.
In a separate Facebook post, La Viña denied the allegations against Leviste and SPBC.
“There is no crime committed here by Leandro Leviste nor his company Solar ng Bayan which was granted a franchise by Congress in 2019,” he said.

La Viña said SPBC was not a public utility covered by the PSA. He also argued that the franchise was never implemented because the DOE failed to issue the necessary rules and regulations and identify the areas where it could be implemented.
Because of this, La Viña said the franchise was “ipso facto revoked,” or automatically revoked under the law.
He also described the DOE complaint as “a complaint looking for a crime.”— MCG, GMA News
