articles.title: Outrage in Japan after U.S. Marine accused of murdering Okinawan woman
articles.summary: A U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman in Okinawa. The killing has drawn outrage on the island and inflamed longstanding tensions over U.S. military…

image.caption: Protesters, many of them Okinawan women, outside the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo on Wednesday after a U.S. Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder. (Christopher Jue/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

A U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman in Okinawa. The killing has drawn outrage on the island and inflamed longstanding tensions over U.S. military bases, which residents say are a source of noise, pollution and violent crime against women.
History of violence by U.S. soldiers against women and girls goes back decades
All her life, 24-year-old Sorane Sakihama has heard stories about crimes committed against Japanese women by U.S. soldiers stationed in Okinawa, Japan.
So when a U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha, Sakihama decided she had to do something.
"As an Okinawan, I don't want to see any victims again," she told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "We have to end this history."
Sakihama helped organize a protest outside the U.S. embassy in Tokyo on Tuesday, where hundreds of people came to demand justice and call for the ouster of U.S. military bases from Okinawa.
It was one of several protests across the country this week.
About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, demanding U.S. bases be removed from the island.
One sign read: "We've had enough of this!"
LISTEN | Interview with protest organizer Sorane Sakihama:
As It Happens6:19Japanese protesters take to the streets after U.S. Marine accused of murdering Okinawan woman

Okinawa police have arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, on Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, ​police said.
Sakihama, who grew up in the town of Chatan, didn't know Yagi personally, but says she has met people who did.
"People say she's a really good, kind person."
Devin Jacob Ballard, a U.S. Marine, has been arrested on suspicion of robbing and murdering Anna Yagi, 39. Police say he denies the allegations. (Kotaro Ueda/Kyodo News/The Associated Press)
The killing has drawn outrage in Okinawa and inflamed longstanding tensions over the military bases, which many locals see as a source of noise, pollution and violent crime.
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from the Second World War until 1972. Today, it is home to 70 per cent of the U.S. military facilities based in Japan, and hosts 18,000 U.S. Marines.
"My grandparents experienced World War II, and what they say is that the military never protected us," Sakihama said.
"They really wanted to have their own land back, but they couldn't."
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the killing "an extremely brutal and vicious incident" and called on the U.S. to co-operate with the police investigation.
History of violence against women and girls

The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases on Okinawa rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to local police. But the history of violence by U.S. soldiers against women and girls goes back much further.
In 1995, the rape of a 12-year-old ​Okinawan girl by three U.S. servicemen sparked mass protests. In 2013, two U.S. sailors pleaded guilty to the rape of a Japanese woman in Okinawa.
In 2016, a worker on a U.S. air force base admitted to strangling Rina Shimabukuro, a 20-year-old woman whose body was found in undergrowth.
In 2024, a U.S. Air Force member was charged with kidnapping and raping a teenager girl in Okinawa, and was later sentenced to five years in prison.
"Nothing has changed," Sakihama said. "[As long as] we have bases in Okinawa, the situation won't change."
Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja, left, speaks to the media in Naha, Okinawa, on Sunday, calling the murder of a local woman 'absolutely unforgivable.' (Kyodo News/The Asscociated Press)
Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said this latest murder underscores the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes.

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."
The U.S. embassy and the Marine ⁠Corps expressed condolences over Yagi's murder and said they were co-operating with the Japanese authorities.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behaviour," it ​said in a written statement.
George Glass, the U.S. ambassador to Japan, wrote on X that he spoke to U.S. military about holding "our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity."
What happens next?
Despite strongly worded statements from Japanese and U.S. officials, Sakihama says she doesn't believe they will remove the U.S. military presence from Okinawa.
"I don't expect anything from them," she said.

Prime Minister Takaichi has been pushing to strengthen Japanese military presence and collaborate with U.S. officers on island, which is viewed by Tokyo and Washington as key in deterring ⁠potential military aggression from ‌China.
A woman holds a sign demanding the closure of U.S. military bases in Japan during a protest outside the Japanese prime minister's office on Tuesday. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images)
The U.S. Marines said Ballard remains in Japanese custody.
His case will be handled by Japanese authorities because he was off-duty when the crime was committed and off base when he was arrested.
Japanese prosecutors will determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, Ballard could face life in prison or the death penalty.
Interview with Sorane Sakihama produced by Nishat Chowdhury. With files from Reuters and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank
articles.summary: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers,…
articles.byline: William Christou in Jerusalem and agencies

blocks.text: Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.

Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.
Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.

His assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.
This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.
Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.

A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.

At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.
A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.
“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.

Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.
The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.
AFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.

“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.
“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.

“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”
Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.
Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.
Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.

Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.
Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

articles.title: Fitness influencer apologizes after hitching a bike ride in the Berlin Marathon
articles.summary: The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" for violating the rules Saturday to her 520,000 followers, explaining…

image.caption: Runners compete during the 2026 BMW Berlin-Marathon on Sept. 27, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Over 56,000 participant from 162 nations took part in the race. And one of them, a Chinese fitness influencer, was photographed riding on the back of a bike for part of it. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" for violating the rules Saturday to her 520,000 followers, explaining that she was feeling physically unwell during the race but that it wasn't an excuse.
Chinese influencer Abeeeer was also dropped by her sponsor, Brooks
There's so much to love about marathon season.
The gripping accounts of elite athletes pushing themselves to the very limit. The tales of runners uplifting and supporting each other to cross the finish line. The heartache when dreams are dashed.
And then there are the people who might think, "Well, maybe no one will notice..." at a global event.
In that vein, a Chinese fitness influencer has apologized and been dropped by her sponsor after being photographed hitching a ride on a bike during the 42.2-kilometre Berlin Marathon last week.

Images of the influencer from the Sept. 27 race were first posted by the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) Instagram account, which calls out questionable race performances. In posts from Oct. 1, the account noted that her fastest time was recorded between the 35- and 40-kilometre marks, around the time "she was spotted on the back of a bike."

A composite image of three Instagram stories posted Oct. 1 by The Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) that allege to show a Chinese influencer hitching a ride in the Berlin Marathon, her times, and a finish line photo from the Sept. 27 race. (@officialunofficialtime/Instagram)
CBC News has reached out to OMTIU to ask how it obtained the photo and to the Berlin Marathon for confirmation, but has not yet received a response.

The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on the popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" to her 520,000 followers Saturday for violating the rules. She explained that she had been feeling physically unwell during the race but acknowledged that was not an excuse.
"My behaviour to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the spirit of the marathon," she wrote in Chinese.
"I intentionally concealed this fact during my public sharing after the race. That was a truly dishonest behaviour."
The bib number shown in the images is registered to Yuanyuan Sun of China, who recorded a finishing time of 4:53:46.

items: Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
Berlin Marathon winner limped to finish line after rupturing Achilles tendon chasing world mark

blocks.text: Multiple media outlets report that she had previously posted about earning a PB, or personal best, on her social media, but has since deleted her Berlin Marathon posts other than the apology.
One of her sponsors, Brooks, confirmed with CBC News that it dropped a runner after becoming "aware of the situation involving a Brooks China collaborator and the 2026 Berlin Marathon."
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual," Brooks told CBC in a statement Tuesday.
"Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition."

A general view as runners compete during the 2026 BMW Berlin-Marathon on September 27, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Over 56,000 participant from 162 nations took part in the 52nd edition of Berlin Marathon. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images)
A short history of marathon cheaters

More than 56,000 runners from 162 countries entered the 2026 Berlin Marathon. It's known for being the flattest course of the official Abbott World Marathon Majors — and therefore the fastest. About 50,000 people crossed the finish line.
And while it's not known whether anyone else attempted a shortcut this year, marathon cheating is nothing new, and what's know as course-cutting is one of the more common tactics.

items: Remembering when Rosie Ruiz stole the Boston Marathon from a Canadian
She was set to win the U.S. women's half marathon. Then a guide car made a wrong turn

blocks.text: One of the more infamous course-cutting examples is Rosie Ruiz, who was the first woman to cross the finish line of the 1980 Boston Marathon. She was crowned with a laurel wreath and didn't even seem tired.

Officials later determined that she had emerged from the crowd near the end of the race and run only about the final mile. She had qualified for Boston after taking the subway for most of the 1979 New York City marathon.
In 2011, Rob Sloan placed third in the U.K.'s gruelling Kielder Marathon. It was later revealed that he had ridden a bus for part of the course.
In 2023, Scottish ultramarathoner Joasia Zakrzewski finished third in a 50-mile race but was later disqualified for riding part of the course in a car.
The same year, the Mexico City Marathon disqualified some 11,000 runners for cutting sections of the course, including by using cars, bikes and public transit.

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. articles.title: How drunk is too drunk? Cornell rape allegations expose 'loopholes' in consent laws
articles.summary: The BBC speaks to experts about current US state sexual assault laws and why some believe changing them will help alleged victims.

blocks.text: A backlash over the handling of a US woman's sexual assault complaint against Cornell University fraternity members has highlighted what experts believe are issues with the current laws in many states regarding sexual assault and drinking.
The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, last month filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped by several men in 2024 at the university in the state of New York.

Doe said she had been drinking earlier in the evening of the alleged incident and then went to a fraternity house, where several men pressured her to snort the drug ketamine and plied her with alcohol before advertising a "free" sexual encounter with her in a group message.
She said she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.
Under current New York law, a person who voluntarily consumes drugs or alcohol - rather than becoming intoxicated without their consent - is not automatically considered unable to consent to sex.
US media has been widely reporting it as the "voluntary intoxication loophole".
New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week said: "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape" and that she would work with the state legislature to close the "loophole".

But some experts say the law has been misinterpreted and that it does not stop people who choose to consume alcohol or drugs from reporting sexual assault. It does, however, require them to prove they were so incapacitated they could not physically consent - a higher bar than being intoxicated.
The distinction reflects an ongoing debate in the US about what counts as consent when someone has been drinking.
Dan Schorr, a former sex crimes prosecutor, told the BBC that New York law still protects victims of assaults who have chosen to drink or take drugs.

"If a person cannot express consent or lack of consent due to the consumption of alcohol or drugs, any sexual activity with them is always non-consensual, whether the ingestion of alcohol or drugs was voluntary or involuntary," said Schorr, who also helps universities review sexual assault cases.
"I prosecuted many people who sexually assaulted someone who was voluntarily intoxicated," he said, adding: "I got convictions. They went to prison."
Some believe issue with the current law is that the bar is set too high with regards to what counts as being too intoxicated to give consent.
At least 19 states, including New York, have a higher bar for the level of intoxication required to deem someone incapacitated and unable to consent.
The New York law includes a provision that someone cannot consent to sex if they are "unconscious or for any other reason physically unable to communicate an unwillingness to an act".
This applies to people who are too incapacitated from drinking to consent, Schorr said.
But another legal expert the BBC spoke to says that can be difficult to prove.

Some prosecutors "may not bring charges or defendants may be acquitted because someone 'gave consent' while intoxicated, but not completely incapacitated", according to Mitchell Epner, a former prosecutor who has handled sex trafficking cases.

He said that in other states that have lower legal bars for incapacitation, someone who is "impaired" or "significantly impaired" cannot consent, and that being too drunk to drive a car could be considered as being at this level.

College campuses have different standards for consent than criminal law, including Cornell, which uses a standard of affirmative consent, defined as "a knowing, voluntary, and mutual decision among all participants to engage in sexual activity". Cornell says silence or lack of resistance does not constitute consent.

Epner supports a proposed change to New York's law to widen the scope of when someone is too intoxicated to consent. The New York Senate has passed a bill multiple times, but the state Assembly failed to bring it up for a vote.

That bill states that people cannot give consent if they are under the influence of substances that have rendered them "temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling" their conduct, and "such conduct was known or reasonably should have been known" to the other person.
Pennsylvania has also made efforts to try and change the law to make it easier for victims who were intoxicated to prove they were assaulted.
"If somebody's too drunk to drive, they're too drunk to - fill in your verb of choice," Epner said.

Representative Lea Webb, whose district includes Cornell University, told the BBC News Channel she and her fellow lawmakers were working to push through legislation on the issue, which has gone through several amendments.
New York's current laws, she said, "puts the onus of proof on the victim".
Schorr and criminal defence attorneys, meanwhile, criticised the proposed changes to New York's sexual assault laws.

New York's State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers said in a statement to the BBC New York's current laws were sufficient, and that "people have been convicted of rape in cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims".

The group said using language that a victim was "incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct" was "simply too vague to be fairly enforced", adding that the legislation does not give clear details on what constitutes someone being too intoxicated to engage in sexual conduct.
Schorr said it was not easy to answer this question of what exact point someone is too intoxicated to consent.
He added: "How should the law address that? It is very challenging to find a clear standard that will be evenly applied."
"It's a conversation we should have as a society, as a state".

articles.title: Big Brother UK sparks backlash after housemates debate trans rights
articles.summary: Viewers of Big Brother UK are criticizing its contestants after the show aired a tense debate about transgender rights, pronouns, single-sex bathrooms and trans athletes in sports.

image.caption: From left to right: Big brother UK contestants Rochelle Rackham, Twinks Burnett and Philip Regan. (Instagram/bbuk/ITV)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Viewers of Big Brother UK are criticizing its contestants after the show aired a tense debate about transgender rights, pronouns, single-sex bathrooms and trans athletes in sports.
Fans on social media split, with some accusing contestants of transphobia

It happened during Sunday night's episode of the reality competition series — one of more than 60 editions of the franchise worldwide — where a group of strangers called "house guests" or "housemates" live together for several weeks in a custom-built house, completely cut off from the outside world. Filmed 24/7, they compete in challenges and survive weekly evictions to outlast everyone else and win a cash prize.

Two new contestants joined the house that night: Twinks Burnett, 36, and Catrin Richards, 23. The debate, which was posted on the show's official social media, began after Burnett started a conversation about LGBTQIA+ allyship and gender identity.
Here's what happened
Housemate Philip Regan, who is gay, said he was in favour of freedom of speech, arguing, "You can't say anything, and it's wrong."
"Me, growing up, my generation, it was 'him' and 'he,'" said Regan, 53, referring to gender pronouns. "Now, everything's different."
He went on to say, "If you want to be classed as a fridge, you're classed as a fridge."

Burnett countered by saying it was "no one else's business to tell you who you are, what your sexuality is and we should never assume who anyone is until they tell you," with which several of the guests, including Regan, appeared to agree.
On the subject of whether transgender women should be allowed to use women's washrooms, another house guest — Rochelle Rackham — said, "I wouldn't be happy with a transgender in the toilet with me."
Burnett concluded that building community was the most important step in bridging these differences.
Microphones picked up another conversation later that night where Regan told another housemate that Burnett was trying to "cause trouble" by bringing up transgender protections.
Viewers call out contestants for exchange
The moment drew calls on social media for the network ITV to reprimand Rackham and Regan, with many accusing the two of transphobia and questioning why the network chose to air the conversation.
In the show's previous season, a contestant received a formal warning from producers for misgendering a fellow cast member.
"Have ITV entirely scrapped the diversity and inclusion training this year?" one user wrote on X.

items: 3rd time's a charm? Big Brother Canada set for TV return

blocks.text: "The homophobia is palpable and the transphobia is obvious! I’m so sorry for a trans person watching this show tonight, I can’t imagine how that’s made you feel," wrote another.

Other fans defended the show's choice, saying that the Big Brother franchise has always sought out to capture raw, unscripted human interactions and that removing the conversation would have amounted to censorship.
"Some of these views aren't great but BB is about getting normal, everyday people with different views to live together, and a lot of people won't have the same views as you," a third wrote.
On the show's Instagram account, some praised Burnett for starting the conversation.
Moment backdropped by U.K. legal ruling

The aired conversation mirrors the U.K.'s polarized landscape on trans issues, with ongoing debates about the legal definition of sex under the country's Equality Act, trans athletes' inclusion in sports as well as access to gender-affirming care.

Last year, the U.K. Supreme Court ruled that the legal definition of a "woman" — defined for anti-discrimination purposes — only applied to those assigned female at birth, excluding trans women. The court said trans people would not be disadvantaged by the decision, though advocacy groups disagreed.

items: British Supreme Court unanimously rules legal definition of a 'woman' excludes trans women's identities
England bans transgender women from playing on women's soccer teams

blocks.text: Soon after the ruling, trans women were banned from playing on women's soccer teams in England.

The controversy also comes as the Big Brother franchise is about to get a Canadian revival. Since debuting in the Netherlands in the late 1990s, the show has been adapted for dozens of countries, finding success everywhere from Brazil to the U.K. and India to Australia.
Following a two-year hiatus, Bell Media announced that Big Brother Canada is officially returning to screens, with a new season starting in April 2027.
The network's deal also includes the 12 earlier seasons of the show, plus the French-language series Big Brother Célébrités.
Anyone who has experienced homophobia, transphobia or is affected by these descriptions can look for support through 2SLGBTQ+ services on the It Gets Better Canada’s website.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca
With files from Reuters, The Associated Press and CBC's Jessica Wong.

articles.title: Government to reveal next steps for medically assisted dying, justice minister says
articles.summary: Justice Minister Sean Fraser says the Liberal government will announce its planned path forward for medical assistance in dying on Wednesday.

image.caption: Minister of Justice Sean Fraser, seen last month, says the government's plan for assisted dying in Canada will be announced on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Justice Minister Sean Fraser says the Liberal government will announce its planned path forward for medical assistance in dying on Wednesday.
Committee recommended against expanding MAID to those solely suffering from mental illness

The government has yet to say how it will proceed after a special parliamentary committee released a report in June recommending that the federal government "indefinitely exclude" people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from applying for MAID.

"I feel confident that we've heard a range of different views in the development of the policy process and will be able to share next steps tomorrow," Fraser told reporters on Parliament Hill on Tuesday.

The government has twice delayed MAID expansion that would include those solely suffering from mental illness after the Superior Court of Quebec struck down the government's original 2016 legislation because it found the law too limiting.
Unless the government intervenes, MAID will expand to cover mental illness in March of next year.
MAID should 'indefinitely exclude' people with mental illness, review urges
"I appreciate that I'm asking for patience, which can be hard at times. Look, it's a serious issue. I want to make sure I take the opportunity to line things up the appropriate way," Fraser said.
The 88-page report came after parliamentarians heard from a number of expert witnesses on whether the country is ready from a clinical, health systems and regulatory perspective.
The report said a common theme across testimony was the "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services."

items: This is why Quebec is the only province where you can pre-approve your death
Why the debate about MAID for mental illness still rages

blocks.text: In its conclusion, the committee pointed to a "divergence of perspectives" on whether Canada is ready to expand eligibility to MAID to those suffering with mental illness.
There is currently a private member's bill before the House that would exclude those suffering solely from mental illness from applying for MAID.
The government could put its support behind that legislation or introduce a new bill. When asked, Fraser didn't indicate which route he is planning to take.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

items: Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks
articles.summary: Israeli communities shattered by Hamas masacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Nir Oz

blocks.text: Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.

He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.
“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”

blocks.caption: Aviva and Keith Siegel were abducted from their home in Kfar Aza in southern Israel by Hamas on 7 October 2023. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.

Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.

The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.
Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.

“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.
The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.

A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.

Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.

In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.

blocks.caption: Shlomo Margalit tends to the graves in the Nir Oz cemetery, a silent testimony to the 7 October attacks. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.

The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.
Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.
In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.
The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.

But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.

“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”

He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”

One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.

When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.
“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”

The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.
“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.

“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”

The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.
For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.

Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”

blocks.caption: Aviva Siegel has written a book about her ordeal, saying it was therapy and an act of celebration. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”

She has written a book, Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.

After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.
He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”
Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.

In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.
Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.
The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.
Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.
“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.

Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.

Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.

A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.

Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation of Palestine.

blocks.caption: The graves of Oded Lifshitz and Alex (Alexander) Dancyg, who were abducted by Hamas on 7 October. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.

Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.
Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.

Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.

“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”

articles.title: Ex-US spy who stashed gold bars in his home admits to $200m scam
articles.summary: David Rush, who also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, had revealed the existence of a "clandestine human source", prosecutors said.

blocks.text: A former CIA officer who was arrested after authorities found hundreds of gold bars stashed in his home has admitted to defrauding the US government in a sprawling $200m (£151m) scam involving fake contracts and real estate.
David Rush, 49, is required to pay restitution to the government and forfeit luxury real estate, cars, watches and other assets tied to his crime as part of the plea deal.
Rush also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, which could have caused "grave damage" to national security.
"The defendant will plead guilty because the defendant is in fact guilty of the charged offense," prosecutors stated in a court filing outlining the plea deal.
The BBC has contacted Rush's lawyer, who declined to comment.

Rush was initially charged with theft of public funds, but has now pleaded guilty to wire fraud. At the time of his arrest, a raid on his home uncovered 298 gold bars that he had received for "work-related expenses".
Court filings around the deal bring new details to light, including that Rush revealed the existence and description of a "clandestine human source" to a foreign official.

"The disclosure of such information could endanger the safety and life of the human source and the US government officers working with the source and jeopardize the US government's ability to recruit human sources, who rely on the US government's assurances of absolute secrecy," prosecutors said in the filing.
In a news release, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said Rush "abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions".

FBI investigators said that between November 2025 to March 2026 Rush made repeated requests for "a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses".

"Rush fabricated a highly classified program to justify the acquisition of luxury real estate in South Florida, which he then intended to resell for personal profit," the court filing laying out the deal states.
Rush "effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny", according to the filing.

He then used "fraudulently obtained" public funds to acquire luxury real estate properties in southern Florida. According to the court filing, part of the scam included hiring an interior designer and purchasing $40,000 worth of kitchen appliances for one property.

The wire transfer charge was related to a $45m transfer that he initiated in January 2026. The plea deal also says that he provided top secret data to "a foreign government official who was not authorised to receive it and had no need to know it".
Along with the gold bars, Rush was also found with $2m in cash and 35 luxury watches.
Prosecutors said Rush was moving funds into commodities that could be easily traded, citing "strong evidence" he was trying to hide the money.
Under the deal, he is also required to turn in the watches and two BMW vehicles, along with the cash and nearly $39m that was seized from his bank account.

A federal judge will set his sentence at a later date, and a hearing has been scheduled for 28 January. The charge carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, but prosecutors noted that the time can be added to under federal law.
In June, US Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cited Rush's professional career in deciding he was a flight risk, and ordered him held in jail pending trial.
"He's in a different position than most people to flee and avoid detection by law enforcement," he said.

Court records do not go into detail about Rush's work for the CIA, and describe him as a former senior executive in a US government agency in Virginia who had top secret clearance and access to classified information.

US media have confirmed his former employment with the CIA. According to The Washington Post, external, he was senior executive in the agency's Directorate of Science and Technology, which develops high-tech spy tools.

He had also previously been accused of fraudulently taking military leave with pay after being honourably discharged from the US Navy, and for lying about his education and military service when applying for his job in 2009. Court records show Rush was accused of falsely telling employers he had been a navy pilot.
"These and other representations concerning Rush's military and academic accomplishments were false," the plea deal filing states.

It is unclear how he was able to lie on his application form, and according to The Washington Post, several CIA officials have been placed on leave as they investigate why he was able to pass a background check.
The government had argued previously that large sums of the funds are still unaccounted for, a claim which his lawyer has denied.

articles.title: French AI company announces new, private model
articles.summary: The company's new model, named "Le Chonk," is its first release in five months. Mistral says it outruns some of its Chinese competitors in several areas.

image.caption: Mistral is considered Europe's top AI companyImage: Shannon Stapleton/REUTERS

blocks.text: Frenchtech company Mistral on Tuesday announced the upcoming release of "Le Chonk," its biggest AIopen-weight model, aimed at users wanting to keep their data private.
Popular AI models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAIrely on closed models.

Le Chonk, officially named Mistral Large 4, will be made publicly available on October 27, with cybersecurity experts and government authorities receiving access to a version of the model with fewer safety restrictions to test its capabilities.
Last month, Mistral raised €3 billion euros ($3.4 billion), Europe's biggest technology fundraising.
The new AI model allows users to download and customize "weights" that determine how it computes on their own servers.
An open-weight model means a user can download the software and run it on their own hardware. While the top US models run on their own models, many of their Chinesecompetitors are open-weight.
Europe's AI hope
Mistral, considered Europe's leading AI company, said the new model outperforms many rival open-weight models.
Le Chonk is the three-year-old company's first new model release since May.
According to Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch, the new model is "actually above the Chinese models" in certain areas, including cyber.
"The narrative that Europe cannot compete is something that is not true," Mensch said at the company's event in Abu Dhabi, without specifying which Chinese models he was referring to.
MIstral has positioned itself as a safer European alternative in comparison to its main US competitors, especially given the latter companies' recent warnings regarding AI's dangers.

Christine Fréchette, Quebec’s outgoing premier, announced Tuesday that she will be stepping down as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec party.
The party failed to win a single seat on Monday night
Fréchette stepping down as CAQ leader after crushing election loss
The announcement comes one day after the party’s crushing defeat in the provincial election that saw it go from a massive majority just four years ago to being wiped off the electoral map.
The party failed to win a single seat on Monday.

She took over as premier following François Legault’s resignation earlier this year, after winning the party's leadership race against Bernard Drainville.

articles.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
articles.summary: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?

blocks.text: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
ByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterReporting fromNew York and Regan MorrisReporting fromCalifornia
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
1. Streaming prices may rise

blocks.caption: Image caption, HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya

blocks.text: Image source, Eddy Chen/HBO
HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.
Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.
While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.
The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.
Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.

While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes".
2. More film releases

blocks.caption: Image caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance
As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.
For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.
That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.
The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.
If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.
Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.
"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.
"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".
Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.
As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.
Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.
3. Hollywood jobs could be hit

blocks.caption: Image caption, Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA

blocks.text: Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA
For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.
Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.
Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".
"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."
A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.
The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.
Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".
She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."
Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.
"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.
4. CNN and CBS could change

blocks.caption: Image caption,  CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building
To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.
The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.
Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.
Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".
"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.
Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.

articles.title: Naked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg
articles.summary: Titled "The Orange Plague," a gold-coated statue presents Donald Trump sitting on a smaller man's back. The Danish artist blamed Trump for getting in the way of efforts to address climate change.

image.caption: The statue of naked US President Donald Trump went on display in StrasbourgImage: Marek Majewsky/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A statue of USPresident Donald Trump was put on exhibit in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France.
The 2.5-meter satirical statue, by Danishartist Jens Galschiot, is called "Orange Plague," and it shows the US leader naked, holding a long gold club and sitting on the shoulders of a smaller man.
The artist said it is coated with 23-karat gold. The statue is also known by the name "King of Injustice."
Next to the statue are cards explaining that the "King of Injustice" is "sitting on the back of a man" who is sinking under the burden.
"I would do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back," the card continues, with the artist blaming Trump for hindering attempts to confront climate change.
No comment from Trump
The statue stands at an intersection connecting two of the parliament's buildings, and is scheduled to remain there until Thursday.

blocks.caption: The European Parliament is located in Strasbourg, FranceImage: Pascal Bastien/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Left-wing Danish European Parliament member Per Clausen, who invited the artist, said he is not worried about a potential reaction by Trump.
"If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage," Clausen said.
The US president has not commented on the statue, which has also been on display in other European cities as well as at the COP30 UN climate conference in Belem, Brazil.
