articles.title: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
articles.summary: Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they called police repression.
articles.byline: Paul Kirby, Hugh Schofield, Nick Beake, Mark Lowen

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.
Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.
Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers.
The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement.
In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction.
A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed.
"Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart."

Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added.
There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases.

One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability".

Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone.
On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens.
Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired.
The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.

What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too.
Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September.

Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.

"We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling.
Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris.

articles.title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
articles.summary:
Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out the necessary environmental impact assessments

Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in…

blocks.text: Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.

The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a 13bn euro project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.
It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330-hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment.
In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.
The Finnish Union for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.

On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.

The environmental impact assessment (EIA) is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.

Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”
after newsletter promotion
If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.
In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and admitted that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.

The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”

Tapani Veistola, chief operating officer at the Finnish Union for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appears to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, is “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”
One of the reasons behind it, he said, is the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.
“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”

articles.title: EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
articles.summary: The European Commission has put forward ideas it hopes will both ease the EU expansion process and allay concerns among existing members. Several countries, not least war-torn Ukraine, are among the…

image.caption: Expansion was a key issue at 'Berlin Process' talks in candidate country Montenegro this month seeking to further Western Balkan integration into the EUImage: Regierung von Montenegro

blocks.text: The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements."

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter.

The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules.

They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion.

blocks.caption: Ukraine is the newest EU candidate country, seeking to accelerate the process amid Russia's invasionImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Why is expansion coming back into focus?
In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum.
But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand.

In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more. But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
What did the Commission say about expansion?
Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion.

"Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us."
She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them."

Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged.
"One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said.
Why the US-EU rift is spilling into the Balkans
What changes are the European Commission proposing?
The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to:

items: Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids
It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however
Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible"

"Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights
Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine

Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments

blocks.text: All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented.

blocks.caption: Moldova's President Maia Sandu is also a staunch advocate of her country joining the EUImage: Vladislav Culiomza/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the current situation with EU candidate countries?
A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves.

Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro, after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028.
Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years.

Ukraine is the newest addition to the list, having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion.
Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership.
A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

articles.title: Russia denies anti-plague measures after pneumonia death
articles.summary: The death of an employee at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk is still being looked into, the authorities said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Russia to be transparent about its…

image.caption: The woman who died worked at an anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk regionImage: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russiadenied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague.
The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region.
The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place.
Authorities deny reports of plague

According to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia.
"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said.
Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early.
Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute.
The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report.

blocks.caption: Irkutsk is at low risk, according to the World Health OrganizationImage: Kirill Kukhmar/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: World Health Organization monitoring situation
The World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk.
Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute.

"Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk.
The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation.
According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world."
Editor: Sean Sinico
Could a Russia plague case trigger wider concern?

articles.title: Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom
articles.summary:
Journalists are calling for an urgent amendment to the Special Operations Bill, which boosts police search and seizure powers

Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent…

blocks.text: Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that boosts police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press.
The government says the Special Operations Bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation.
The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention and search and seizure.
But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops.
In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.

Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected.

The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”.

Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”.

Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening.

“One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.”

The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting.

“If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.”

He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to an investigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian which said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”.
after newsletter promotion
“My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.”

Pedro Cárdenas of press freedom and human rights organisation Article 19 expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said.
He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws.
The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment.

Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, branded the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”.
He warned that the government’s past use of emergency powers — including detaining citizens without charge — showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.

articles.title: Greek prime minister pledges to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles
articles.summary:
Kyriakos Mitsotakis said his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, had been supportive of restitution efforts in the past

The Greek prime minister has pledged to “ramp up” his country’s claims to…

blocks.text: The Greek prime minister has pledged to “ramp up” his country’s claims to win back the Parthenon marbles from the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis insisted he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.

“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the 5th century BCE marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.

“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”
Mitsotakis also conceded, for the first time, that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of chair George Osborne, had failed to make headway.

Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected to Burnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, more than 200 years ago.

“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.
“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe.”

The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.

Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with officials in Athens seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of the row finally ending.

In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”

“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”

The British Museum has been home to around 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.

Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, insisted Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.

There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the national archaeological museum in Athens allowing gems that had never before seen outside of Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.

“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”

articles.title: France’s conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
articles.summary: Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding…

image.caption: Protesters outside the Lycee Sophie Germain in Paris: French students are calling for better conditions in schools as the government seeks to save billionsImage: Eric Baradat/REUTERS

blocks.text: France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.
At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.
On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.
Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu (left) and Education Minister Edouard Geffray both face increasing pressure as student protests continueImage: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.

Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.
A signal to the markets

Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.
Student protests in France: Schools shut as unrest grows

"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.
No majority in sight for the budget

The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.

blocks.caption: There is currently no majority in the French parliament for the austerity budgetImage: Isa Harsin/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.
More money for schools — and more protests

The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.

blocks.caption: Many young people are angry about the state of the education systemImage: Nacho Doce/REUTERS

blocks.text: For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.
Financing education is getting more costly

The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."

Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.
France students demand better schools

Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.
Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.
Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns

In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.

From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.
A French problem with a European dimension

France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.

blocks.caption: Student protests are increasingly being overshadowed by violence. The signs are visible at many schools including the Lycee Vauquelin in ParisImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Philippines, Poland ink mutual legal assistance pact
articles.summary: The Philippines and Poland yesterday signed an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, as leaders of both countries expect expanded relations in economy, information technology,…

blocks.text: October 7, 2026 | 12:00am

President Marcos shakes hands with Poland President Karol Nawrocki at Malacañang on October 6, 2026. This marks the first-ever state visit by a Polish head of state to the Philippines since diplomatic relations were established in 1973.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Poland yesterday signed an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, as leaders of both countries expect expanded relations in economy, information technology, defense as well as a strategic partnership amid security threats facing the two nations.
President Marcos welcomed Polish President Karol Nawrocki and his delegation at Malacañang, where the latter was accorded arrival honors.
This is the first visit of a head of state of the Republic of Poland to the Philippines.

At a joint press conference at Malacañang, Marcos highlighted the two countries’ ongoing and future cooperation in key areas such as defense and security, trade, industry, agriculture, science and technology, information and communications technology, energy, legal cooperation and people-to-people relations.
The President also cited the Philippines’ acquisition of S-70 Black Hawk combat utility helicopters from Poland as part of the modernization program of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

He said the two countries look forward to building on the outcomes of the inaugural Philippines-Poland Joint Defense Cooperation Committee, including through joint training and educational opportunities.
Poland has been participating as an observer in the Balikatan Exercises since 2025.

“President Nawrocki and I also had insightful exchange of views on regional and international matters of mutual concern, including the challenges in the South China Sea and security developments in Ukraine and in Europe,” Marcos said.
“We reiterated our shared commitment to upholding the rule of law in international relations and the peaceful resolution of conflicts,” Marcos said.

For his part, Nawrocki said defense cooperation is an important aspect of the two countries’ relations, as security challenges face by Europe and the Indo-Pacific “can no longer be approached separately.”
“We want to develop this cooperation also in other areas,” the Polish leader said, noting that the IT sector is one of the important areas of potential cooperation between Warsaw and Manila.
“We have discussed maritime security, state resilience, cyber security, also about the security of strategic supply chains,” Nawrocki said.
“Today we want, and we are opening a new chapter in these relations. Poland is very much interested in raising our relationship to the level of a strategic partnership,” he noted.
Marcos said he and Nawrocki reaffirmed the two countries’ respect for international law.
“And of course, these incursions or attempts to change territorial definitions are unacceptable in both Poland and in the Philippines,” he said.
Nawrocki will inaugurate today the fifth edition of the Polish-Filipino Economic IT Summit in Manila.
He also asked the Philippines’ support for Poland’s permanent membership in the G20, as it is the 20th largest economy in the world, and has invited Marcos to visit Warsaw.
The two countries signed the Agreement on a Transfer of Sentenced Persons earlier this year.
Manila and Warsaw also affirmed their readiness to commence negotiations on an extradition agreement, Marcos said.

articles.title: Government urges SC: Junk petition vs BSKE postponement
articles.summary: The Supreme Court should dismiss the challenge to the law fixing the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections officials and resetting the election to November 2028, as well as deny efforts…

blocks.text: October 7, 2026 | 12:00am

High school students sign up for the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections at the Commission on Elections satellite voter’s registration site at the Pinaglabanan Elementary School in San Juan, in this file photo from August 2025.
Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should dismiss the challenge to the law fixing the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) officials and resetting the election to November 2028, as well as deny efforts to prevent its enforcement, several government agencies appealed.

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), which represented the Office of the President, the Senate, the House of Representatives and the Commission on Elections (Comelec), filed on Oct. 5 its 64-page comment to the petition for certiorari and prohibition submitted by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal.

The comment disputed Macalintal’s arguments in his petition filed on Sept. 27, including his claim that Republic Act 12326, which fixed the term of barangay and SK officials from four to five years and rescheduled their election to November 2028, “infringes the electorate’s right of suffrage by postponing the November 2026 BSKE under the guise of fixing terms.”

RA 12326, signed into law by President Marcos on Sept. 24, moved the next regular BSKE from Nov. 2, 2026 to the second Monday of November 2028 and set succeeding elections every five years. It also fixed the term of barangay and SK officials at five years.
“RA 12326 is a valid term-fixing law. Hence, the 2023 Macalintal guidelines do not apply to the present case,” the OSG declared.

The agency referred to RA 12232, which set the term of barangay and SK officials to four years and scheduled the election to the first Monday of November 2026, in justifying the validity of RA 12326 that scheduled the next BSKE to the second Monday of November 2028.

“Like RA 12232, the main purpose of RA 12326 is to extend the terms of BSK officials from four years to five years. The resulting postponement of elections is but a logistical consequence of the term extension,” according to the OSG.
It also maintained that Congress has the discretion to set the terms of barangay and SK officials.

“It is a political question which brings to the fore the wisdom of the law, taking into account both Congress’ role as legislators and as representatives of the people keenly aware of the realities at the grassroots level,” said the OSG.
TRO urgently sought
Macalintal, however, renewed his plea for the SC to stop the implementation of RA 12326.
In an urgent omnibus motion and reply filed electronically with the SC yesterday, Macalintal reiterated his request for a temporary restraining order and/or status quo ante order.

He also asked the court to direct the Comelec to resume preparations for the Nov. 2 BSKE or, if the polls could no longer be held on that date, conduct them on a date reasonably close to it under the Omnibus Election Code.

Macalintal disputed the government’s interpretation, pointing to Section 5 of RA 12326, which states” “Considering the extension of their terms by two (2) years, incumbent elective barangay officials shall be regarded as having completed one (1) term in their respective positions.”
“If this is not an extension of the term of incumbent barangay officials, then what is?” Macalintal said.
He argued that Congress’ authority to determine the term of barangay officials does not include the power to prolong the existing term of incumbents after they have been elected.

Macalintal also rejected the government’s characterization of the 2028 election date as merely an “incidental setting,” arguing that moving an election to a later date constitutes a postponement when it keeps incumbents in office beyond the period for which they were elected.

Macalintal also disputed the government’s reliance on governance continuity and multiyear projects, saying these reasons did not satisfy the standards previously laid down by the SC for postponing elections.
He challenged the administration’s reasons for retaining incumbent barangay officials, including their role in crime prevention, flood response and garbage collection. — Christine Boton

articles.title: ICC prosecutor opposes evidence disclosure cap in Duterte’s case
articles.summary: The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court has opposed the request of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s lawyers to limit the documents disclosed in relation to his upcoming crimes…

blocks.text: October 7, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has opposed the request of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s lawyers to limit the documents disclosed in relation to his upcoming crimes against humanity trial.
In his 16-page response released yesterday, ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang maintained that the documents disclosed to the defense are reasonable and relevant to the case.

He was responding to defense lawyer Peter Haynes’ allegations that the prosecution provided them with a “sheer volume of material” that supposedly undermines Duterte’s right to adequate time for preparation of his defense.

“The prosecution rejects the repeated portrayal of the disclosure of documents that memorialize the attack against the civilian population, including victims specified in this case, as the ‘dumping of documents’ into the case record,” read the prosecution’s response.

“The prosecution’s disclosure is further reasonable, considering the large geographic and temporal scope of this case and the fact that the accused is a former head of state who openly ran a ‘war on drugs’ that drew significant domestic and international attention. The volume of the prosecution’s List of Evidence is also consistent with that of other cases at this Court,” it added.
In his original request, Haynes asked the Trial Chamber III to act on what it described as “voluminous” documents disclosed by the prosecution ahead of the trial.
He noted that from the initial 5,275 items of evidence during the confirmation phase, the prosecution has now expanded it to 62,130 items.

“The defense has no ability to read this volume of evidence prior to trial. However, even a cursory review demonstrates that much of the disclosed material is of extremely limited or no relevance to the charges in this case,” said Haynes.
Niang, however, responded by pointing out that majority of its disclosure came from a dataset containing “highly relevant” information.
He said the prosecution has taken reasonable steps to help the defense review the dataset, including summaries of incidents in the documents.

“Setting an arbitrary cap on the number of documents the prosecution can disclose would automatically place the prosecution in violation of its disclosure obligations as it would require the prosecution to withhold evidence that it considers material to the defense’s preparation,” wrote Niang.

“The prosecution respectfully submits that withholding material evidence from the defense, or forcing the prosecution to remove a dataset that directly supports the contextual elements of its case, would more severely hinder the search for the truth in this case,” he added. — Bella Cariaso

articles.title: P50 million from other countries flowed to Duterte-linked firm
articles.summary: Apart from China, eight other countries – some of which are notorious for money laundering – had been the sources of nearly P50 million in remittances that flowed into a food company…

blocks.text: October 7, 2026 | 12:00am

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo asks Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Atty. Ronel Buenaventura if he is still nervous while testifying during the second day of the impeachment trial on October 6, 2026.
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — Apart from China, eight other countries – some of which are notorious for money laundering – had been the sources of nearly P50 million in remittances that flowed into a food company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio.

Records flashed on screen yesterday on Day 34 of the impeachment trial of Duterte showed that inflows of funds to CALE88 Foods Corp. also came from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Lithuania, South Africa, Tajikistan, the United Arab Emirates and the United States.
Senator-judges pressed for a breakdown of the foreign funds and questioned the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) if it had ever moved to freeze the accounts.

Based on data flashed by House of Representatives prosecutors, CALE88 received P12.8 million from Russia, P12 million from Ukraine, P7.24 million from Kazakhstan, P6.23 from Lithuania, P6 million from South Africa, P3.8 million from Tajikistan, P684,456 from UAE and nearly P600,000 from the US.

Sen. Raffy Tulfo grilled AMLC executive director Ronel Buenaventura on whether the AMLC had ever unilaterally petitioned the Court of Appeals (CA) for a freeze order on CALE88’s accounts or demanded contracts justifying the purpose of the deposits.

Tulfo also questioned why the council did not flag the non-Chinese inflows despite the reputation of some of the countries as money laundering haven. “Don’t you find it suspicious that a large part of the funds that went to CALE88 came from countries with critical reputation for money laundering like Russia, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, South Africa, di ba kayo nagduda doon?”

Buenaventura declined to make conclusions and apologized to the court. “I have no personal knowledge on the current status of the countries mentioned or their financial or money laundering standing in the international community,” he said.
Requirement
He also said during direct examination by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia that banks are required by law – not just encouraged – to report all suspicious transactions to AMLC.
“The law used the word ‘required.’ So they’re required to report suspicious transactions. The law did not mention any threshold. The law says regardless of the amount,” Buenaventura said.
“A suspicious transaction could be higher than the threshold or it could be lower than the threshold, as long as the presence of suspicious circumstances are there,” he said.

“Essentially, suspicion is one based on the knowledge of the covered person or reporting entity, based on the profile of the client and taking account all other circumstances to determine whether or not there is a suspicious circumstance,” Buenaventura said.
“The threshold, at least insofar as the law requires, is suspicion or suspicious circumstances,” he added.
But defense counsel Mark Vinluan insisted that such bank records are covered by the confidentiality rule.
“Covered institutions are required to report suspicious transactions. They are not just encouraged to report suspicious transactions,” Divinagracia said in response. — Delon Porcalla, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
articles.summary: The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease.

blocks.text: Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood.
Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.
Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.
It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague.
The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases.
Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.
Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.
He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world.
"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa.
"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."
Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal.

But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.
You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.
It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.
Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague.
"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said.
"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.
"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism.
"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."
According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.
If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.
But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early.
Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health.
"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease.
"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age.
"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early.
"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."
In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague.

The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.
US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States".
The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

articles.title: UK: Seventh arrest made after air base plot
articles.summary: The man, a British national in his twenties, was arrested in London in suspicion of "preparing terrorist acts."

image.caption: The US military's B1 bombers were withdrawn from RAF FairfordImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in the UK arrested a man in connection with an alleged planned attack on a military air base used by the United States.
The suspect, a 22-year-old British national, was arrested "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts," police said.

Police arrested the man in London, and he is the seventh person taken into custody in connection with the incident in which three vans were stopped near the RAF Fairford air base in England's southwest on September 27.
While no explosives were found in the van, police secured some gasoline in them, it said.
The other six suspects were also men in their 20s, including one who is a dual UK-Iranian national. All six have been released on bail.
Media reports in the UK said one of the initial suspects had informed the authorities of the incident, which police did not confirm.

blocks.caption: Police were alerted to suspicious activity next to the RAF Fairford baseImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bombers withdrawn
US bombers have been seen taking off and landing at the air base, with the UK government allowing Washington to use it for "specific defensive operations into Iran."

US President Donald Trump said Washington had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford due to "threats" possibly linked to Iran. At the same time, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down specific threats.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said there were "strong indications" that Iranhad a role in the incident, with British authorities labeling it "major." The UK also insists the RAF Fairford air base is safe.
Tehran rejected any involvement.

articles.title: Munich up against at least six competitors for 2036 Olympics
articles.summary: The International Olympic Committee has revealed the six other countries intending to bid for the 2036 Olympic Games. This comes after Germany selected Munich as its Olympic candidate.

image.caption: Munich hosted the 1972 Summer Olympic GamesImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Munich's bid for the 2036 Summer Olympics will be up against at least six candidates from Europe, Asia, and Africa. On Tuesday, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced that, in addition to Germany, Hungary, Turkey, India, Qatar, South Korea, and South Africa all intend to bid for the Games. All are currently engaged in the "Continuous Dialogue" stage of the bidding process with the IOC.

However, there could be further applicants, as the deadline for interested parties to submit a bid is October 31. The candidates are to present their plans virtually to the Future Host Commission in November. In March 2027, the IOC is to deliberate, analyze, and narrow down the field of applicants to a group selected to enter into the Strategic Dialogue stage.
A subsequent Targeted Dialogue stage with one or more bidders is planned for 2028, with the final decision on the 2036 Olympic host expected at the IOC Session in the summer of 2029.
However, the IOC did not disclose exactly which cities, alongside Munich, are in the running – although Ahmedabad, Doha, Budapest, and Istanbul are seen as possible hopefuls.

Munich secured its bid late last month after beating the Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr region in a vote by delegates of the German Olympic Sports Confederation. The city last hosted the Games in 1972. Berlin had withdrawn its bid in the days leading up to the vote.

blocks.caption: As a swimmer Kirsty Coventry won two Olympic gold medals for ZimbabweImage: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: 'Best possible experience for the athletes'
"Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do," IOC President Kirsty Coventry said.

"As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life," added the former swimmer who won gold in the 200-meter backstroke for Zimbabwe at the 2004 Athens and 2008 Beijing Summer Games.
"That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point."
Munich bid sees itself as well-positioned

The IOC is to evaluate the bidders' proposals based on "technical factors." These include a master plan for competition venues and the athlete experience, the financing strategy, political and public support, the capacity to deliver the event, and a sustainability strategy. The German Olympic Sports Confederation believes Munich is well-positioned in all these areas.

The Munich bid is not focused solely on 2036 but was also designed with 2040 and 2044 in mind. If it misses out on 2036, Munich can expect to face a similarly large pool of competitors for the following two Summer Games. According to an IOC statement, there are National Olympic Committees "taking part in noncommittal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036."
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: Germany shaken by espionage and treason allegations
articles.summary: The former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, has been accused of spying for a foreign country. Never before has a German official of August Hanning's stature been accused of…

image.caption: Former BND chief August Hanning has been arrested on espionage chargesImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: If the allegations are confirmed, it would be an espionage case of historic proportions for Germany: August Hanning, former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), has been arrested, with the federal prosecutor accusing him of espionage, treason and attempted treason.

August Hanning, now 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. But even before then, he had enjoyed a meteoric rise within the security apparatus. After leaving the BND, he served as state secretary in the Federal Interior Ministry, then moved into the private sector and worked as a security consultant.

According to the federal prosecutor's office, his informant was his former chief-of-staff, named in the statement only as Manfred D.*, who went on to hold this position under Hanning's successors from March 2012 to March 2026. D. thus had access to a great deal of classified information.
Former German spy chief arrested for espionage
Classified information from the chancellor's office

Manfred D. is alleged to have passed on nearly 2,000 BND documents — some of them highly sensitive — to Hanning over the course of several years in exchange for money. Hanning is then said to have used the information in his private consultancy business.

The most serious allegation is that Hanning is said to have maintained close contact with an employee of a foreign intelligence service for years and to have leaked classified information to him. It is not known which country was involved, but reports say it is not Russia.

Investigators also mention an analysis that Hanning is said to have prepared for an employee of another foreign intelligence service. However, it is not certain whether the analysis ever reached that person.

The classified information also concerned the routine meetings of the heads of German security agencies at the chancellery. Topics included, among other things, the Iranian nuclear program and analyses of the Russian armed forces.

Since intelligence from foreign partner agencies is also said to have been shared in this context, this could also undermine their trust in the German BND and lead to difficulties in future intelligence cooperation with Germany.
Hanning came under scrutiny in an entirely different context
"A good agent is one who doesn't draw attention to himself," Hanning was once quoted as saying. When he finally drew attention to himself, it was in an entirely different context.

In September 2025, the Hamburg state police searched Hanning's home and offices in connection with the famous case of the kidnapping involving Christina Block, heiress to the steakhouse restaurant chain Block House. State prosecutors in Hamburg accused her of having ordered the kidnapping of her two youngest children in late 2023 due to a custody dispute.

A little over a year before the operation to bring the children back, there is said to have already been a failed kidnapping attempt. At the time, there were suspicions that Hanning was involved, which he denies.

But during a search in 2025, investigators found an electronic storage device containing top-secret BND documents. The police handed the documents over to the federal prosecutor's office, which launched a covert investigation against Hanning and Manfred D. in May 2026. The most recent documents found so far are said to date from June 2022.
Greens demand consequences

Throughout its history, the BND has seen a number of espionage cases, some of them spectacular. In the 1960s, Heinz Felfe headed the "Counterintelligence: Soviet Union" division while simultaneously working for the Soviet secret service, the KGB.

In 2014, a BND employee was exposed as a spy for the US CIA. There is also an ongoing trial against a BND agent accused of betraying secrets to Russia's FSB in September and October 2022 — that is, after the start of the war in Ukraine. Yet never before has a former official of August Hanning's stature been at the center of suspicion of espionage.

"The BND launched extensive internal investigations early on and without delay, which corroborated the suspicions," said current BND President Martin Jäger. "For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security."

However, there was some fierce criticism from the political sphere. Günter Krings of the conservative governing party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told the Rheinische Post newspaper: "The mere suspicion that a former BND chief is selling secrets is damaging to trust in our security agencies."

Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party and deputy chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services said: "These are serious and grave allegations that have been leveled against August Hanning." Speaking on behalf of his party, he called for greater scrutiny of lobbying activities by former top officials and those with the highest security clearances. "These are clearly also a gateway for hostile intelligence services," von Notz said. The federal government must put an immediate stop to these "illegitimate practices."

Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the socialist Left Party group in the Bundestag, went even further: "The investigations against former BND chief Hanning show once again: The intelligence services themselves are a security risk."
This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

articles.title: Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant
articles.summary: Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival…

image.caption: 'That's all folks,' Warner Bros. and Paramount and their subsidiaries will all be bundled under a new banner: Skydance Corp.Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.
The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.
The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.
Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?
The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.
The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.
Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.
Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.

Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

articles.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom called the remarks "deranged", but the White House said Trump was warning of the risk of a nuclear Iran.
articles.byline: Jamie Whitehead & Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter

blocks.text: Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.

California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at an election campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.

While speaking in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, he said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was "disgusting and disqualifying".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".

"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".

The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.

A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.

San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.

articles.title: Spain court lifts Puigdemont arrest warrant, clearing way for his return home ahead of November elections
articles.summary: Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont fled Spain in 2017 after launching an independence bid. The court's decision means he can return home without fear of arrest after almost a decade in exile.

image.caption: The 63-year-old has been wanted by police since 2017Image: Glòria Sánchez/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: Spain's Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted an arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, paving the way for him to return home ahead of a general election next month.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after leading a failed attempt for the wealthy northeastern Catalonia region to break away from Spain.
He had been wanted by authorities ever since, accused of embezzling public funds to hold an illegal independence referendum when he was head of Catalonia's regional government.
Judge Pablo Llarena lifted the arrest warrant shortly after Spain's Constitutional Court ruled that a 2024 amnesty for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement cases.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the decision, saying it would allow Catalonia to "look to the future."
"We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time," he told journalists in Madrid.
How did the amnesty come about?
While Puigdemont and other members of his government fled abroad after the 2017 independence bid, several Catalan ministers who remained in Spain were sentenced to lengthy prison terms.

In 2024, in the face of strong opposition from Spain's conservative and right-wing parties, the Sanchez government passed an amnesty law. It intended to cover all offenses related to the secession attempt and ease tensions in the Catalonia region.
It also allowed Sanchez to secure the backing of Catalan separatist parties and stay in power after a 2023 election produced no clear majority.
But Puigdemont's Junts party withdrew its support last year, accusing Sanchez of failing to fulfill promises such as providing amnesty for its leader.

Around 400 separatists have benefited from the amnesty, but Puigdemont had been excluded because Spain's Supreme Court initially ruled the law did not apply to those accused of embezzlement. That changed after the Constitutional Court on Tuesday sided with one of Puigdemont's allies who had appealed against the top court's ruling.
Last week, Junts voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez's government amid huge protests, prompting the prime minister on Monday to call a snap vote for November 29.
