articles.title: Southeast Asia's haze crisis: Have lessons been learned?
articles.summary: Eleven years after catastrophic fires prompted promises of tougher action, Southeast Asia is again choking on transboundary haze, raising questions about whether the region has learned the lessons of…

image.caption: Indonesia's long 2026 dry season, coupled with this year's El Nino, has worsened what has become an almost annual crisisImage: Willy Kurniawan/REUTERS

blocks.text: Indonesia's worst wildfire season in more than a decade is exposing how much, and how little, Southeast Asia's response to haze has changed since 2015.

Forest and land fires have burned across parts of the Indonesian islands of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua for weeks, sending smoke across large areas of the country and into neighboring Malaysia and Singapore.

Indonesia's long 2026 dry season, coupled with this year's El Nino, has worsened what has become an almost annual crisis, exposing millions of people to hazardous smoke containing harmful microscopic particles.

More than 170,000 cases of acute respiratory infection were recorded in haze-affected areas of Indonesia between August and mid-September, according to the country's Health Ministry, including more than 40,000 cases involving young children.
The haze has forced hundreds of schools to close in Malaysia and pushed more than 1.4 million Indonesian students into remote learning, although the full economic cost is not yet known.

blocks.caption: The haze has spread to Malaysia and forced hundreds of schools to closeImage: Arif Kartono/AFP

blocks.text: Will severe haze become more frequent?

This year's severe weather is only part of the explanation. Fire has long been used as a cheap way to clear land for agriculture in Southeast Asia, while the expansion of palm oil and pulpwood plantations has drained and degraded large areas of peatland.

The echoes of 2015 are hard to ignore. That year's fires burned roughly 2.6 million hectares of land, produced months of severe haze across Southeast Asia and cost Indonesia an estimated $16 billion (€14.2 billion) in economic losses, according to the World Bank.
The risk is growing that severe haze will become more frequent as climate conditions worsen, Paruedee Nguitragool, an associate professor at Chiang Mai University in Thailand, told DW.
"Haze, which used to be mainly a problem in maritime Southeast Asia, has become a concern for most countries in the region," she added.
Governments within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the regional bloc, "need to be more open to one another and work closely together."
"Farmers and companies need alternative methods of land clearing and incentives to adopt them, while land and forest rehabilitation must also be implemented," Nguitragool said.
"At the same time, consumers need to be more aware of whether the products they buy come from sustainable practices and whether burning was involved in their production," she added.

blocks.caption: Fire has long been used as a cheap way to clear land for agriculture in Southeast AsiaImage: Reina/AFP

blocks.text: What changed after 2015?

The 2015 disaster triggered major policy changes. Indonesia strengthened peatland restoration, fire monitoring, enforcement and firefighting, while ASEAN expanded regional cooperation, David Mark Taylor, a professor of tropical environmental change at the National University of Singapore, told DW.

Indonesia established the Peatland Restoration Agency in 2016 to restore millions of hectares of degraded peat. Its mandate was later expanded to mangrove rehabilitation, with the agency renamed the Peatland and Mangrove Restoration Agency.
A permanent moratorium on new concessions in primary forests and peatlands also restricted further development in some vulnerable areas.

Authorities have also increasingly pursued companies in court. Last year, an appeals court ordered palm oil company PT Banyu Kahuripan Indonesia to pay around €14 million in environmental damages over fires covering more than 3,300 hectares of its concession. Other companies have faced much tougher restoration orders.

At the regional level, ASEAN adopted a new Peatland Management Strategy and a second Haze-Free Roadmap for 2023-2030, and the long-awaited ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control opened its secretariat in Jakarta in April, more than two decades after the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
"But the underlying problem hasn't gone away, and neither has the driver," said Taylor.

Extensive areas of peat remain drained or degraded, including cleared land that has yet to be put into productive use. Such poorly managed or "idle" peatlands can become highly combustible during prolonged drought, Taylor noted.
There is also disagreement over how much restoration Indonesia has actually achieved.

The Peatland and Mangrove Restoration Agency ceased operating at the end of 2024, with its responsibilities returned to other government ministries and institutions, raising questions among environmentalists about whether they can maintain the same institutional focus.

ASEAN faces its own limitations. Its 2002 haze agreement is legally binding, but many targets and implementation plans depend on national governments acting on them. The regional bloc has few mechanisms to compel governments to meet those targets or punish failure.
But the ultimate driver for all of this "is the global demand for cheap, plantation-grown commodities, such as palm oil and pulp and paper, which most of us are responsible for," said Taylor.
"So long as that demand persists, so too will the pressure to convert peatlands and forests to plantations," he added.
Indonesia's battle with slash and burn farming
Can ASEAN stop the next crisis?
This year's fires have turned attention from creating new agreements to how Southeast Asian governments can make existing mechanisms work.

"To prevent this from worsening further, there needs to be a real pooling of capacity among ASEAN. Indonesia, for all its efforts, does not have the capacity to manage it alone," Helena Varkkey, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, told DW.

The existing ASEAN mechanisms for joint emergency response should be operationalized, she added, but this should have been arranged before the start of the haze season, as meteorological reports made it clear that a "Super El Nino" was comingearlier this year.

"Southeast Asian governments need to work together to prevent biomass-burning episodes by implementing stringent laws to stop peat and forest fires. They need to use all available technologies together to prepare for dry conditions," Mohd Talib Latif, a professor at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, told DW.
"Haze needs to be considered a disaster for this region," he added.

articles.title: As more Iranian women reject hijab rules, regime looks at new ways to force compliance
articles.summary: As more women in Iran reject Islamist rules on wearing hijab headscarves, hardliners are shifting focus from "morality police" street enforcement towards social pressure in workplaces, services and…

image.caption: Iran's regime pushes strict distinctions for women considered to be 'properly veiled' Image: Vahid Salemi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Women appearing in public without wearing a hijab has become an increasingly common sight across Iran, marking one of the most visible social changes since the 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests, which were sparked after a woman died in police custody after she was arrested for allegedly wearing her headscarf improperly.

Authorities have been unable to restore the level of street enforcement that existed before the protests. But the relative retreat of so-called "morality police" patrols does not mean the compulsory hijab has disappeared.
Now, authorities and conservative groups are experimenting with different ways to resist that change without necessarily recreating the same street confrontations that helped fuel the 2022 protests.

Judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni-Ejei recently called for action against what he described as social "abnormalities," "indecency" and "nudity," urging prosecutors to coordinate with police, intelligence bodies and government institutions.

At the same time, supporters of hijab mandates have circulated online campaigns encouraging people to avoid businesses run by women who do not follow the state dress code and instead patronize women who do.
The result is a more fragmented form of enforcement, moving in some cases from police patrols toward workplaces, businesses and access to everyday services.
Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement?
Iran's regime turns to social pressure
The online campaigns call for what supporters describe as "conscious purchasing," encouraging consumers to support hijab-observing vendors.
A female lawyer in Tehran told DW that such campaigns risk deepening social divisions rather than encouraging adherence to a social norm.
"This is a deliberate attempt to categorize people by identity and put them against one another," she said under condition of anonymity for safety concerns.
She argues that encouraging economic pressure against people solely because of their appearance goes beyond an individual's right to choose where to shop.

"When economic sanctions are imposed on them [the regime], they call it pressure, injustice and economic warfare," she said. "But when they use the same logic domestically to force part of society to change its behavior, it becomes 'support for values.'"
She also questioned the assumption that women who conform to one particular dress code uniquely represent Iranian social values.
"The reality of Iranian society is much more complex than that," she said.

Accounts posted by Iranian women suggest that dress-code enforcement can also appear in everyday services, with some women reporting on social media being denied access to clinics and banks for not wearing a headscarf.

blocks.caption: The death 22-year-old Jina Mahsa Amini in 2022 symbolized the Iranian regime's oppression of womenImage: UGC

blocks.text: When women's bodies become political
Shirin Shams is an exiled Iranian political activist and director of the Women's Revolution Organization, which advocates for secularism, women's liberation, and human rights in Iran.
She told DW the recent campaigns targeting women who ditch the compulsory hijab are an attempt to revive social divisions that were weakened during the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement.
"The Islamic Republic has tried for years to divide women according to their clothing," the Germany-based activist said.

She describes the compulsory hijab as one of the Iranian state's most important ideological lines and argues that the widespread presence of women without headscarves shows how far social reality has moved beyond official expectations.
The renewed campaigns, in her view, are about more than clothing, representing an effort to reconstruct a boundary between women who comply and those who do not.
Saeed Paivandi, a professor at the University of Lorraine in France, says the conflict reflects a broader struggle over social control.
He told DW that Iranian authorities have spent years creating distinctions between women considered properly veiled and those officially labeled "badly veiled" or "unveiled."
"The government is once again turning women's bodies into a social, moral and even security issue," Peyvandi said.

A woman without a headscarf is not interpreted merely as someone making an individual choice, he said. For parts of the political establishment, she can also represent a visible challenge to an ideological order.
'I will be living proof of the violent oppression in Iran'
Iran's hardliners vs. modern reality

While Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has repeatedly spoken about social cohesion and national unity, conservative Islamist judicial and political figures continue to demand tougher enforcement of dress regulations.
This produces an uneasy balance and exposes differences within Iran's political establishment.

Parts of the establishment appear aware that a return to large-scale confrontations between police and women could carry significant social and political costs. Others are unwilling to accept the normalization of women appearing in public without wearing a hijab.
The result is neither the old system of comprehensive street enforcement nor an end to compulsory dress rules.
Instead, pressure can appear intermittently through courts, workplaces, businesses, administrative procedures and social campaigns.

blocks.caption: In 2022, protests erupted across Iran after a woman died in the custody of the 'morality police"Image: AFP

blocks.text: Enforcement without the 'morality police'
Paivandi believes direct coercion has reached its limits and that supporters of Islamic dress codes are looking for alternative ways to enforce conformity.
That could shift part of the burden from state institutions to society itself.
A bank employee, clinic receptionist, employer, shopkeeper or customer can become involved in enforcing standards even without a police officer being present.
This makes the boundary between law, personal discretion and ideological pressure increasingly unclear.
Peyvandi also warns that linking religion to humiliation, exclusion and coercion could further alienate younger Iranians from religious institutions.
Women who choose to wear a hijab may also be drawn into a confrontation they did not choose, he said, if their clothing is presented as a marker of political loyalty.

articles.title: N.L. spent millions renovating old college for future courthouse — now it's slated for demolition
articles.summary: After pausing work at the Martin Gallant Building in Stephenville Crossing this past summer, the Newfoundland and Labrador government says the building needs to be demolished, axing plans for it to…

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

After pausing work at the Martin Gallant Building in Stephenville Crossing this past summer, the Newfoundland and Labrador government says the building needs to be demolished, axing plans for it to become the new courthouse and provincial government services building. Mayor Lisa Lucas is now worried about what it means for her community.
Stephenville Crossing mayor says she's worried about future of her community
Teardown order concerns Stephenville Crossing mayor
After millions of dollars were spent redeveloping an old college building on Newfoundland’s west coast, the Newfoundland and Labrador government says it’s now set to be torn down.

In June, the province announced it was pausing work at the Martin Gallant building in Stephenville Crossing after spending $5.6 million. It was once home to the College of the North Atlantic and was planned to be the new courthouse and provincial government services building in the community.

On Monday, the provincial Department of Transportation and Infrastructure said following additional environmental and structural assessments, it had been determined the building needed to be demolished.
Stephenville Crossing Mayor Lisa Lucas says the decision has her worried about the future of her community.
"The current premier wants to go down in history as being the person that signed our community's death warrant," Lucas told CBC Radio’s Newfoundland Morning.
"I'm not going to be surprised if six months from now or seven months from now the PC government announces the new courthouse is going up in Stephenville."

In its statement, the department said further investigation showed the project would be significantly more complex and expensive than previously anticipated. It also pointed to the presence of contaminated soil, lead paint and structural deficiencies.
Lucas said she wants the province to act quickly to demolish the site, citing safety concerns.
"We want that down, and we want it down now if they're deeming it — this— unsafe."
She called the site a "prime piece of real estate" and wonders what will happen to it now.
Residents were previously excited when plans to redevelop the building for government services were announced by the previous Liberal government — which has now turned to fear, she said.

In the past, Lucas said the town has had a good relationship with the region's MHA, regardless of political party, but it seems there’s a lack of transparency and communication with the PC government.
The previous Liberal government had started renovating the Martin Gallant Building after concerns were raised about the accessibility of the provincial building in nearby Stephenville.

In a previous statement to Radio-Canada, a Department of Transportation spokesperson said the government had previously estimated the redevelopment would only cost $8 million. But after work started, the price tag went up, and in May 2025 a $28.6-million contract was awarded.

The statement went on to say the most recent cost projections went up to $40 million, and the contractor raised concerns about "significant challenges" due to only having a "partial design" at the time of tender.
'A fiasco'
Speaking at an unrelated announcement in Corner Brook Tuesday morning, Wakeham called the project “a fiasco,” pointing to how the project's price tag ballooned.
“And then we now find out that there were structural issues with it and the grounds contaminated,” Wakeham told reporters.
He said they have to figure out if the site can be used for any other purpose in the future.
“My minister will be reaching out to communities and we’ll look at where we go in terms of future developments,” said Wakeham.
Premier Tony Wakeham says given the state of the site, they have to figure out if it can be used for any other purpose in the future. (Amy Feehan/CBC)
'Serious concerns'
Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure Barry Petten is expected to speak with CBC News Wednesday in an interview.

items: After spending $5.6M, N.L. hits pause on Stephenville Crossing courthouse development
Roughly $2.6M spent on Cartwright school before N.L. government halted project

blocks.text: In Monday’s statement, Petten said upon review of the redevelopment, there were "serious concerns" over its feasibility and cost, adding further review has highlighted problems with the project that should have been known before it was undertaken.

"Had these conditions been identified and assessed earlier in the process, the scope, cost and viability of the project could have been more accurately evaluated from the outset," Petten said in the statement.
"While this is disappointing news, it would not be responsible to continue pursuing a project that no longer represents a sound investment of public funds."
The government is assessing other available spaces in the region for government services.

Corrections

items: This story previously contained a reference to Lisa Lucas being the mayor to Stephenville. In fact, she is mayor of Stephenville Crossing.Oct 06, 2026 1:11 PM EDT

articles.title: Canada's trade surplus widens to more than 4-year high in August, as front-loading ramps up
articles.summary: Canada's trade surplus with the U.S. hit a 19-month high in August, Statistics Canada reported on Tuesday.

image.caption: Transport trucks are seen in Aulac, N.B. (CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New
Canada's trade surplus with the U.S. hit a 19-month high in August, Statistics Canada reported on Tuesday.
Exporters shipped more to ​the U.S. to beat looming 50% tariffs from ​Trump administration

Canada's trade surplus widened substantially in August to $4.2 billion, data showed on Tuesday, as exporters rushed to increase shipments to the U.S. before President Donald Trump's new tariffs took effect.
Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast the trade surplus would expand to $1.55 billion, from an upwardly revised $787 million.

As exporters shipped more to ​the U.S. to beat the looming 50 per cent tariffs, Canada's exports stateside surged 8.1 per cent in August, while imports from the U.S. were down 2.5 per cent, Statistics Canada reported.

This change helped Canada post a trade surplus with the ​U.S. of $11.2 billion, a 19-month high, lifting its share of exports to its biggest ⁠trading partner to almost ⁠70 per cent for the first time since September 2025.
Trump's new ‌tariffs, which cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports to the U.S., came into effect on Aug. 22.

Economists have said that September would show a more accurate impact of the new tariffs, which apply to a variety of items, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods ⁠and hockey equipment.
September will also show the impact of Canadian counter-tariffs on U.S. imports and Trump's ban on some goods imports from Canada.
Canada's overall exports increased by 2.5 per cent in August to $77.91 billion, after falling by 2.6 per cent ‌in the previous month.

Exports of energy products — refined petroleum products and crude oil — posted the biggest overall gain, increasing by 4.7 per cent to $19.03 billion. A stronger Canadian dollar also affected the value of exports.
Consumer goods, machinery exports up
Excluding energy products, exports were up 1.8 per cent. In volume terms, total exports rose 2.5 per cent, StatsCan ​said.

Exports of consumer goods were up 6.6 per cent, industrial machinery, equipment and parts were up 10.1 per cent and electronic and electrical equipment and parts increased 11 per cent ⁠in August, the statistics agency said.
Imports were down two per cent to $73.71 billion, with imports of motor vehicles and ⁠parts posting the largest decline in August.

As Canada negotiated waves of tariffs across some crucial sectors ⁠such ⁠as steel, aluminum, autos and lumber for ​almost 18 months, its export dependence on the U.S. had shrunk, while exports to the rest of the world ​rose, as it sought to ⁠diversify its trade partners.

After increasing 8.2 per cent in July, exports to countries other than the U.S. fell 8.5 per cent in August, and imports decreased. Its trade deficit with countries other than the U.S. widened to $7 billion in August from $5.3 billion in July, StatsCan said.
The Canadian dollar strengthened after the trade data, with the currency trading up 0.05 per cent ⁠to $1.4250 to the U.S. dollar, or ‌70.18 U.S. cents.

articles.title: Russia responds to US help offer after death of plague researcher
articles.summary: The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases.

blocks.text: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has urged people not to "listen to various rumours" after a Russian lab technician died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Peskov called for people to follow only information from Russia's public health watchdog, which named the official cause of death of the lab technician as pneumonia of unknown origin.
BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg also asked Peskov about US President Donald Trump's offer of support to Russia.

articles.title: Tigray war may spill over to Eritrea — helped by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's rhetoric
articles.summary: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed is consolidating power, but he must contend with a regional alliance opposing him and a Tigray conflict that could spill over into Eritrea.

image.caption: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was on Monday sworn in for a new five-year mandateImage: Ethiopian PM Office

blocks.text: Amid escalating conflict in Ethiopia's northernmost Tigray region, Abiy Ahmed has been sworn in for another term as Prime Minister of Ethiopia.
Shortly after the ceremony on Monday afternoon, Abiy reiterated his will to work toward giving the landlocked country direct access to the Red Sea.

"Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea," Abiy said, a remark that risks exacerbating tensions with neighboring Eritrea. The two countries have been at odds over Ethiopia's desire to control Eritrea's port of Assab.
DW correspondent Solomon Muchie, who followed the swearing-in ceremony in Addis Ababa, said despite the renewed mandate, Abiy faces challenging times ahead.

"The new term gives Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stronger political authority," Solomon said. "But the country's complex internal and regional challenges could make it difficult to translate the authority into lasting stability."

Sunday's meeting in Cairo of countries that opposed Ethiopia was a case in point, Munchie said. "The leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan discussed regional issues, but Ethiopia was excluded from this meeting, so this is also what Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government will face in his tenure in the coming years."
Ethiopia still eyeing Eritrea's port of Assab

For analyst Abdurahman Sayed, who leads the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, Eritrea now faces an imminent threat of entering the war in Tigray. This comes after a three-year Ethiopian campaign to gain control of the port of Assab.

"Eritrea has legitimate concern of Ethiopia's intentions to occupy [the country] if it can, and then if not, then at least take the port of Assab, which is a very important port, not only for commercial purposes but also strategically," Sayed said.

"It oversees the Bab el Mandeb [Strait], which is the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Now, without that port, Eritrea's strategic significance would be reduced to almost nil, so there wouldn't be any importance of Eritrea."
Last week, Ethiopia severed its diplomatic ties with Eritrea and Egypt. According to Sayed, this might be a sign that the government is determined to pursue its push for the Red Sea port by force.
The renewed fighting in Tigray might point in that direction. Just days ago, the Ethiopian National Defence Forces took control of Tigray's capital, Mekelle.

On Monday, a pro-government media outlet reported that the Ethiopian army had begun mobilizing its troops towards the Eritrean border, following a movement of the opposed Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) retreating to the area near Adigrat, an important gateway to Eritrea and the Red Sea.

blocks.caption: The pro-government Tigray Peace Force got a warm welcome from the Mekelle population after the takeover on SundayImage: AFP

blocks.text: "The Tigrayan people have cultural, linguistic and religious links with those in southern Eritrea," Sayed said. "In fact, the ones in power in Eritrea have many more similarities with those in Tigray."
He added that there could be a spillover effect, especially now that the TPLF is out of Mekelle, and they might be out of major towns as well. "So they might go for a kind of ragtag fighting tactic."
According to Sayed, the Ethiopian government and army are only waiting for Eritrea to enter the war.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict

"They've already been making allegations without substantiating them, without any evidence, that the Eritrean army is already in Ethiopia fighting against the Ethiopian government. Although the truth is the Ethiopian rebel movements, they are quite well experienced in fighting, and they have plenty of armaments and so on," Sayed said.

"So there is not much need for the Eritrean army to be there physically to support them. But the Ethiopians would love to see that, so they can justify their attack on Eritrea by claiming that they were the first one to be attacked, and therefore they were now responding to that attack."
Calls for diplomacy

While allegiances in the Horn of Africa region and the Near East have been much debated in the context of the recent crisis, actors from the global North have remained relatively silent — though experts like Abdurahman Sayed have welcomed a statement by the United States for diplomatic efforts to be renewed.

blocks.caption: Fighting has also been going on in Afar region, slowly moving towards the route that links Djibouti to Addis AbabaImage: Tigray Peace Forces Public Relation Department

blocks.text: One decisive factor, then, might revolve around access to Djibouti, the one Horn of Africa country with which Ethiopia has long been on good terms. At a recent webinar by the independent conflict monitor ACLED, the institution's senior East Africa analyst, Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, elaborated on this.

"Ethiopia's main trade route is through Djibouti, and that is why we're seeing one of the fronts being within [Ethiopia's adjacent region] Afar. Just like in the previous war, the TPLF wants to control the main route from Djibouti to Addis Ababa," Jalale said.
She also said that, since Israel officially recognized Somalia's autonomous Somaliland region as an independent state, the past year has brought a new dynamic to diplomatic relations in the Horn.
"This also includes Djibouti sometimes aligning with Eritrea, Egypt and so on, but they're also trying to remain neutral," Jalale said.
At the moment, however, both Ethiopia and Djibouti seem to be determined to maintain the trade from which they both profit.
Thousands flee to Djibouti from Yemen's war

"There is also hyperinflation in Ethiopia," Abdurahman Sayed said. "And if there is a shortage of supplies and oil, that can cause major pressure on the Ethiopian government between yesterday and today."

Also, Djibouti, located strategically at the entrance to the Red Sea, hosts many international airbases, including those of the US, China, France, Italy, and Japan. Cutting off the country's trade route to mainland Africa could be the tipping point that finally prompts international players to speak up and pressure Ethiopia to end the conflict.

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD makes history again in Saxony-Anhalt
articles.summary: For the first time since the end of World War II, a German state parliament has chosen parliamentary speaker from the far right: Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD).

image.caption: AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund (r) congratulated Tobias Rausch (l) on his election as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: First thing in the morning, about 500 people gathered on Cathedral Square in the center of Magdeburg, the capital of the state of Saxony-Anhalt, to send a clear message that October 6 is not just another ordinary day. "Against Forgetting — Fascism Must Remain a Crime," read one of their banners. "No cooperation with the far right," read another.

Directly across from the imposing cathedral, in the state parliament building on the other side of the square, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected as speaker of the state parliament at 12:40 p.m. He received 48 votes — 9 more than the number of seats the AfD holds in the state parliament.

And this marks a turning point not only for Saxony-Anhalt but for all of Germany. For the first time since the end of World War II, a German state parliament has elected as its president a representative of a party that the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, has classified as right-wing extremist.
'The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is a right-wing extremist party'

The parliament's inaugural session was opened by Eva von Angern, a member of the socialist Left Party and the senior-most member of the parliament, who had earlier been outside participating in the demonstration across the square. She noted that only a few women in German history had held such a high office. Among them, Von Angern said, was communist Clara Zetkin, who served as senior member of the Reichstag in 1932 — shortly before the Nazis seized power.

Nobody in the AfD caucus showed any support for these words. "Human dignity shall be inviolable," Von Angern then quoted from Germany's Basic Law. This includes, she added, people of different genders, worldviews, religions and skin colors. And she quoted former Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker. "He said: 'One expresses one's own dignity by respecting the dignity of others.'" Once again, no one in the AfD expressed any enthusiasm.
Allegations of nepotism against Rausch

Tobias Rausch, a 35-year-old real estate agent, is little known outside of Saxony-Anhalt. Many observers describe him as relatively approachable, and he describes himself as "not a hardliner." However, his name made headlines nationally at the beginning of the year when numerous AfD politicians were accused of nepotism.

Rausch himself admitted to employing several of his friends from his soccer club in his legislative office. That did not prevent his caucus from nominating him as president of the state legislature. Officially, the office is the highest-ranking position in the state.

After his election as parliamentary speaker, Rausch asserted: "I will not serve in this office as the speaker of a single parliamentary group, but as the speaker of all parliamentary groups." He added: "Rules must apply even when the majority changes."
After AfD's record result: voices from Saxony-Anhalt
A large AfD bloc — in the center of the chamber

Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the seating arrangement of the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The AfD parliamentary caucus — composed of 37 men and two women — had taken its seats in the center, keeping a firm gaze on the lectern. The fact that this can be intimidating is clearly intentional.

Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The parliamentary caucus — composed largely of men — seated itself prominently in the center where they could keep a firm eye on the lectern. Observers remarked that this can be intimidating.

Unlike in other parliaments, where the far-right party would normally sit far to the right, it has positioned the "old parties" that it despises — namely the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the socialist Left Party and the environmentalist Greens — around the edges. The AfD was able to push this seating arrangement through in preliminary talks before the state parliament convened to vote. The message is clear: We are the center. A new era has begun in Saxony-Anhalt.
A regional election that drew international attention

The election that took place on September 6 of this year in Saxony-Anhalt was certainly the most closely watched regional election in Germany in many years. Several hundred journalists, including several from international media, traveled to Magdeburg for the election.

Among the 1.7 million eligible voters in this German state, located between the Elbe River and the Harz Mountains, one thing was clear months before election day: the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which has been partially classified as right-wing extremist — would emerge as the strongest party. Some polls even predicted that the party would secure an absolute majority of the votes.
In the end, the AfD garnered 39 of the 83 seats, just shy of the 42 seats it would have needed for an absolute majority.
Added together, the CDU, the Left Party, the SPD and the Greens also come to a combined total of 39 seats.

The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht, holds just five seats and yet could be the deciding factor in whether AfD's top candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, can actually become the state premier. The BSW had announced that it would vote for Rausch as parliamentary speaker, but not for Siegmund as head of the state government.

Nevertheless, Siegmund plans to stand for election in the state parliament in December. It will again take place by secret ballot. Siegmund has been displaying confidence, saying he intends to win in the first round of voting. And if he fails, he intends to call fresh elections.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground

On this point, the new parliamentary speaker, Tobias Rausch, commented on private TV channel RTL the morning before his election: "If we don't have a majority in the first round of voting, we won't have a majority for the rest of the legislative term either — in that case, it means the parliament doesn't want us to govern." Whatever happens, Saxony-Anhalt is facing turbulent times ahead.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Nobel Literature Prize: How the winner is secretly chosen
articles.summary: Can Xue is considered one of this year's favorites; Margaret Atwood and Salman Rushdie are other strong contenders. But what goes on behind the scenes in the selection of the Nobel Prize in…

image.caption: The building of Nobel Prize Museum in Stockholm is also the home of the Swedish Academy, which selects the recipient of the literature awardImage: Steffen Trumpf/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Thursday, October 8, at around 1 p.m. CEST, all eyes in the literary world will be set on Stockholm.

That's when the new permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, will hold a press conference to announce the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, marking the end of a lengthy selection process that officially began a year earlier.
Nobel Prize in Literature: How nominations work
The Swedish Academy is the body responsible for awarding the prize. Its 18 members consist of writers, professors and intellectuals.
In September of the previous year, the Academy's Nobel Committee sends forms to hundreds of individuals and organizations eligible to submit nominations for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

According to the Nobel Prize website, these include professors of literature and linguistics at universities and colleges, previous Nobel laureates in literature and the heads of writers' associations that represent the literary community in their respective countries. Anyone from one of these groups who has not received a form may also submit a nomination.

"The list can reach 200 names per year of nominated authors," explains Gisele Sapiro, research director at France's National Centre for Scientific Research. She studies how the Nobel Prize, as a global institution, influences the international circulation of literature, power dynamics in the literary world and translation markets.
"The committee can also add names itself, such as authors who were nominated in previous years," she says.

In the spring, the Nobel Committee then selects five names through a multistage process and presents them to the Academy. Over the summer, Academy members read the nominees' works and discuss them. The decision is always announced in early October.
As for the criteria the Academy uses to make its decision — it prefers to keep them to itself.

blocks.caption: The 2026 laureate? Chinese author Can Xue holds the best bookmakers' oddsImage: Dave Johnston/EEm/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Nobel Prize in Literature's secret files
The public doesn't learn which nominees missed out until 50 years later — that's how long the Academy waits before releasing the list.

Sometimes decades pass between an author's first nomination and actually receiving the prize. Danish writer Johannes V. Jensen, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1944, waited 40 years. Doris Lessing received the award in 2007 after 35 years, while Thomas Mann, who won in 1929, had to wait 27 years.

blocks.caption: According to the Academy, Thomas Mann received the award in 1929 primarily for 'Buddenbrooks'; the novel had already been published in 1901Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In his will, Alfred Nobel, the founder of the prize, stipulated that it should be awarded to the person who had produced "the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction." That leaves plenty of room for interpretation.

According to Gisele Sapiro, the Academy's aim is to honor ambitious, influential literature that has, for example, given rise to a new literary movement. "At the same time, the work has to be universal, being able to transcend their own culture," she says.

Translations can be one indication of this. "I noted in my research, however, that all the laureates since 1990 had been translated into English, French and German," Sapiro explains, "except for Abdulrazak Gurnah [Editorial note: the Tanzanian-British 2021 Nobel laureate], who had not been translated into German before winning. Meaning that I think these three languages are the most important."
Sapiro says it is also a major advantage if nominees have already won other major literary awards, such as the International Man Booker Prize, the Cervantes Prize or the Büchner Prize.
Any genre is eligible
Politics can also influence the Swedish Academy's decisions.

On several occasions, the prize has gone to writers who openly opposed the regimes in their home countries, such as Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich in 2015. She is an outspoken critic of Alexander Lukashenko.

Genre, on the other hand, does not matter. In the past, laureates have been honored not only for novels but also for poetry and plays. In 2016, singer-songwriter Bob Dylan received the prize for his song lyrics.

So far, only 33 of the 122 laureates have come from outside Europe. There is also a clear gender imbalance. Only in the past eight years have men and women alternated as winners, significantly increasing women's share of the total number of laureates — to 14.9%.
This article was originally written in German.
Why Stephen King will never win a Nobel Prize

articles.title: US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in Israel
articles.summary: Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in…

blocks.text: A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in Jerusalem advertises a talk from the Trump administration’s anti-terrorism czar alongside speeches from far-right Israeli politicians, European figures who have faced disciplinary action over alleged antisemitism, and Christian nationalist and far-right figures from the United States.

The Jerusalem event is perhaps the most significant recent gathering to feature large contingents of Israeli nationalists alongside Christian nationalists and far-right European nationalists from a milieu sometimes shadowed by accusations of antisemitism.

Sebastian Gorka, a senior White House official whose May anti-terrorism strategy promised to target and neutralise groups “whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist”, was scheduled to speak at the Jerusalem event, and his presence is still advertised on the website.

But when the Guardian contacted the White House for comment on Gorka’s attendance at the conference, a spokesperson advised that he would no longer be attending due to a scheduling conflict, and that he had condemned Hamas’s 7 October attack on Israel.

blocks.caption: Sebastian Gorka at the AmericaFest 2024 conference, sponsored by conservative group Turning Point in Phoenix, Arizona, on 20 December 2024.   Photograph: Cheney Orr/Reuters

blocks.text: From Israel, the program lists Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, self-declared “fascist homophobe” and internationally sanctioned extremist, and Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, who in 2023 called for an atom bomb to be dropped on Gaza and was earlier ordered to face disciplinary proceedings for racist incitement against Palestinians.
The Guardian contacted both men for comment.

From Europe come Hans-Georg Maaßen, who once led Germany’s domestic intelligence agency but in 2023 faced an expulsion attempt by his then party, the CDU, for “statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues”, and Austria’s Harald Vilimsky, whose far-right Freedom party has been subject to a policy of non-engagement by Israel’s own government.

According to Israeli media reports, Vilimsky has played a key role in building a rapprochement between the Freedom party – whose first two leaders after its founding in 1956 were former SS officers – and Tel Aviv. He has visited the country repeatedly and in January reportedly led a European delegation to the country that was received by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, despite criticism from Austria’s own Jewish community.

In a statement, Maaßen wrote: “I firmly reject the claim that I made ‘statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues’. This deliberately vague wording was never a concrete accusation but a politically motivated label, designed to damage my reputation and to discredit critics of the political mainstream of the time,” Vilimsky was also contacted for comment.

blocks.caption: Hans-Georg Maaßen, former head of the Germany domestic intelligence service takes part in a constituency meeting of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) district associations in Suhl, eastern Germany, on 30 April 2021.  Photograph: Jens Schlueter/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The American contingent includes William Wolfe, a self-described Christian nationalist who has called for “mass deportations, denaturalizations, and remigration” to preserve a white Christian majority, and Jonathan Keeperman, the publisher unmasked by the Guardian in 2024 as the man behind the far-right internet persona “L0m3z”.
Keeperman did not address questions sent to him when asked for comment. Wolfe did not respond directly to questions on his attendance at NatCon, instead sending personal insults.

Dr Brendan McGeever, co-director of Birkbeck University’s Institute for the Study of Antisemitism, said: “Many attendees at NatCon view Israel not just as an ally but as an embodiment of the exclusionary ethnostate they wish to establish. National Conservatism sees in Israel a blueprint for the realization of a white, Christian nation built on racialized exclusion, while far-right Israeli attenders at NatCon often argue that partnering with white Christian nationalists is the best way to protect Israel. It is racism that binds these forces together.”

Attenders will also share a stage with high-profile conservatives including Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts, and former deputy national security adviser Victoria Coates, who is now vice-president at Heritage’s Davis Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy.
The Guardian contacted Heritage with questions about their attendance at NatCon.

Last October Roberts defended Tucker Carlson after the broadcaster gave a friendly interview to the white nationalist and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, saying in a video that “the venomous coalition attacking him are sowing division”. He later called the phrase “a terrible choice of words”, and said he and Heritage would speak out against antisemitism. In July a Heritage spokesperson said the thinktank’s “record opposing antisemitism is long, consistent and public”. In May, Heritage elected Yoram Hazony to its board.

blocks.caption: Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts introduces former vice-president Mike Pence during an event to promote his new book at the conservative thinktank on 19 October 2022 in Washington. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: Roberts and Wolfe are among the NatCon Jerusalem attenders singled out last month by the evangelical conservative commentator Erick Erickson, in a broadside against “a group of white guys” who “have subtly inserted themselves into conservative institutions and church organizations” and who “to varying degrees … embrace white nationalism, antisemitism”.

Erickson’s principal target was the shampoo tycoon and would-be “warlord” Charles Haywood, the subject of extensive previous reporting in the Guardian, but he also singled out Heritage fellow Scott Yenor, another Jerusalem speaker. He was supported in his efforts by other NatCon attenders, including the writer Rod Dreher.
The Guardian contacted Haywood and Erickson for comment.

Matthew Taylor, a senior visiting fellow at the Georgetown Center for Faith and Justice and author of the new book Defying Tyrants, said: “I think they were trying to find a way to kind of carve out a version of Christian nationalism that could synchronize with kind of European and Israeli politics … and I think what they’re discovering is kind of the impossibility of that.”

He added: “[Hazony is] running up against the limits of that project because the reality is that you can’t simply stir up abstract Christian nationalism. One side of the Christian nationalist coalition is very aligned with Israel, is very Christian Zionist, the other side is leaning hard into this antisemitic impulse.”

The gathering is the latest in a series of NatCon conferences held in the United States and abroad since 2019 by the Edmund Burke Foundation, whose founder is the Israeli nationalist and rightwing intellectual Yoram Hazony.
The conferences are high-profile gatherings of the international national conservative movement, which scholars describe as the most influential strand of an anti-liberal “New Right”.

Past NatCons have featured JD Vance, Viktor Orbán, Giorgia Meloni and Nigel Farage, and have drawn accusations of racism and extremism since a speaker at the first Washington conference argued for an immigration policy of “more whites and fewer nonwhites”. Conference organizer Hazony, reportedly said at that time that the speaker’s views were “legitimate and should be heard and debated”. In 2024 a Brussels mayor ordered police to shut the event down before a court overturned him.
The Guardian contacted Hazony for comment.

Gorka is listed for a 7 October plenary titled “The Meaning of October 7”, alongside Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, and the former Polish president Andrzej Duda. The Guardian previously reported on a video in which Gorka offered Israeli leaders advice on Hamas: “Kill every single one of them. God bless Israel. God bless Judeo-Christian civilisation.”

In August 2024 Smotrich said of Gaza: “Nobody will let us cause 2 million civilians to die of hunger, even though it might be justified and moral, until our hostages are returned.” Britain sanctioned him on 10 June 2025, acting with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway. It held him responsible for “inciting, promoting and/or supporting” abuses, “in particular acts of aggression and violence against Palestinian individuals in the West Bank”.

Rabbi Eliyahu, who for decades has served as chief rabbi of Safed, a public office in Israel, remarked of Palestinians in Gaza in a lecture his office posted to YouTube in November 2023, “Drop an atom [bomb] on them? It’s an option,” he said. The disciplinary hearing Israel’s high court ordered in 2020 was reportedly not held until June 2024, and its outcome kept from the public.

The conference’s co-sponsors include the Sovereignty Movement and Regavim, the organisation Smotrich founded. The ultranationalist Israeli television news outlet Channel 14 says it is producing the event with Hazony’s foundation and his Herzl Institute. The conference website does not currently list the channel as a partner.
The Guardian contacted Channel 14 for comment.

One panel is titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement”. Maaßen’s talk is billed as “Why Elites Embrace Mass Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation”. A fellow panelist, Nathan Pinkoski of the Center for Renewing America, wrote the introduction to a 2025 edition of The Camp of the Saints, a novel Dreher at one time called “racist”. Dreher appears to have since softened that view.
The Guardian contacted Pinkoski for comment.
Vilimsky reportedly told a Budapest conference in April 2024: “We do not want Mohammed to become the most common name in our countries.” He is listed for a NatCon plenary on 7 October.

Gideon Sa’ar, the foreign minister, who last month welcomed a speech by the FPÖ leader, Herbert Kickl, at a Strasbourg event Vilimsky organised with Likud, as making possible “a substantive, open and sincere dialogue” despite the ongoing disengagement, is listed for the conference dinner on 6 October.

Wolfe told a Texas audience in February: “My boys all look like me. And I want my children to grow up in a country where they’re not minorities.” He has called Erickson’s essay “a call for the assassination of a group of conservative Christians”. His conference bio says he served at the state department and the Pentagon in the first Trump administration.

As previously reported in the Guardian Haywood’s private foundation gave the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organizes the NatCon conferences, $25,000 for “general operations” in the year to June 2023, its tax filing shows.

Hazony’s former communications director was among the Jewish conservatives who criticised him in January, after he blamed an “antisemitism-industrial complex” for failing to make the case against Tucker Carlson. He has since refused Carlson a speaking slot in Jerusalem, and on 28 September called the broadcaster’s show “the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America”.

Taylor, the religion scholar, said: “[Hazony is] still trying to play an older game of drawing boundary lines and saying, oh, there is an antisemitic far right that is the fringe that we have to cut off … But Tucker Carlson is not [fringe]. Tucker Carlson is about as mainstream today in rightwing politics as you can get.”
The Guardian contacted the Carlson Network’s press office for comment.

McGeever, the antisemitism scholar, wrote: “Yoram Hazony may express bewilderment about this surge of antisemitism, but it is baked into the very political alliances he has forged. His allies have repeatedly promoted ideas about ‘globalist elites’ and ‘secret cabals’ which utilize the same structural logic of antisemitic conspiracy theories.”
The conference runs from 6 to 8 October at Jerusalem’s International Convention Center.

articles.title: Argentina to stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, country’s foreign minister says
articles.summary: Pablo Quirno says move is part of government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islands Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that…

blocks.text: Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.

During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.

Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.

Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.

He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.
“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”

blocks.caption: At the UN general assembly last month, Javier Milei condemned the oil development in the North Falkland Basin as an ‘unlawful act’. Photograph: Heather Khalifa/AP

blocks.text: Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.

On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.

The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.

blocks.caption: Javier Milei and Pablo Quirno at the UN last month. On Monday, Quirno warned third parties not to assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of natural resources. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.

The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian govenment rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.
In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.
A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.

Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

articles.title: Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza
articles.summary: Benjamin Davis appealing against dismissal from FAO, after being accused by director general of playing ‘political games’ A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week…

blocks.text: A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week for his work highlighting hunger in Gaza, and has launched an appeal against his dismissal.

Benjamin Davis said the leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) had refused to renew his contract as director of its rural transformation and gender equality division because his team had published a brief on hunger in Gaza and held a seminar on the subject last year, and because he had taken part in weekly “moment of silence” vigils on FAO grounds for those killed.

The seminar on hunger in Gaza last September triggered a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO, which also sent a diplomat to take pictures of staff taking part a moment of silence gathering last October, according to a FAO staff report filed at the time.

Davis, 62 and a Spanish-American dual citizen, left the FAO last week after 26 years of service. Video of the event shows FAO staff standing and applauding him as he left the Rome headquarters for the last time.

“It’s a nice feeling that I’m not alone, that other people are behind me in this,” Davis said. “I was stopped constantly in the hallways by people, even those that I didn’t know, just to shake my hand or just to thank me or just to say that they supported me or that they were upset.”

The FAO did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday, but the organisation’s director general, Qu Dongyu, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal in public remarks last Tuesday, in which he threatened to fire more people for what he deemed to be political activism.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Davis had worked for the FAO for 26 years before his dismissal. Photograph: Giuseppe Carotenuto/FAO

blocks.text: “We are not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” said Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist. “Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva. If you want to take care [of human rights], go there.”

“Thats why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him,” he said, suggesting that Davis had violated staff regulations. “I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many. I’m going to use my last year … to fire more if they’re against the law.”
Davis said he and fellow FAO staff members had been stunned by Qu’s remarks.

“Even more than the threat about firing people was just what he said about human rights. I think that really shocked people because it undermined the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists,” he said.
“We’re surely an organisation which is based on human rights, right?” Davis added, pointing to the FAO slogan: “Leave no one behind.”

The official letter informing Davis that his contract would not be renewed said that Qu was “no longer confident in your ability to discharge your obligations in the manner required of a senior international civil servant”.

The letter cited paragraphs in the official code of conduct for international civil servants regarding “honesty, truthfulness, impartiality and incorruptibility” and limits on public expression of personal views on “controversial matters”.
In his written response, Davis said that approach taken by FAO leadership was “simply wrong”.

“Silence in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity,” he wrote. “Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate. Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.”

Davis said that FAO leadership had previously criticised him for a briefing paper published by his team in May last year describing the level of hunger in Gaza and setting it in the context of international humanitarian law.

“The current conditions in the Gaza Strip … reflect a gross violation of the right to food and the unlawful obstruction of humanitarian assistance,” the report said. It was removed from the FAO website a few weeks later on the orders of its leadership.
Davis led a seminar on the same subject in September 2025, which led to a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO and other Rome-based international agencies.

Davis said he had also been criticised for taking part in moment of silence gatherings held by concerned staff in the FAO car park every Thursday, in remembrance of those in Gaza who had died of hunger. There was an altercation there on 23 October when a woman identifying herself as an Israeli diplomat appeared and took photographs of those attending.

“The person explained she was the permanent representative of Israel, and asked if we were allowed to do these events, and asked specifically who says we could not take photographs,” a report by a FAO witness on the day of the incident said.
On being told she could not take photographs, the woman complained to FAO security that she was being harassed, the report said. The Israeli embassy in Rome said it had no comment on the report.

Davis said that the Gaza briefing paper, the associated seminar, and the weekly moments of silence had all been approved by FAO management, and he had not been told at the time that they represented violations of the code of conduct. He said he had lodged a formal appeal against his dismissal.

“I filed the appeal mostly as a matter of principle, not because I’m looking for or expecting any monetary compensation or anything like that,” Davis said. “I have requested to be reinstated, and also for them to take back the accusations that they made against me.”

articles.title: Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
articles.summary: The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Russia has sparked claims about a lab accident, hundreds of infections and international spread. Some of these viral narratives are…
articles.byline: Monir Ghaedi, Tetyana Klug, Anwar Ashraf

image.caption: The image was published by the Irkutsk institute. However, the institute did not respond to questions about the laboratory’s current biosafety measuresImage: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dozens of people were reportedly placed under observation after a laboratory worker at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and other infectious diseases died of severe pneumonia.

The case quickly became the subject of intense speculation on social media. Posts have ranged from expressions of fear and comparisons with the COVID-19 pandemic to claims about the laboratory incident that have not been substantiated.
DW Fact Check has examined several of the claims circulating online.
Alleged plague lab accident in Irkutsk remains unproven

Claim: "For those who don't get it: in Irkutsk, a lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus and became infected with the disease, dying a few days later," a user posted on X in Russian. "This happened on September 25, and by October 2, she was already dead. In the meantime, she had infected several hundred people." The post, which included a photo of the alleged laboratory worker, garnered over 320,000 views.
DW Fact check: Unproven
There is no independent evidence confirming that a leak of the plague pathogen occurred at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.

blocks.caption: "A lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus." The claim has spread widely online, but remains unproven.Image: x.com

blocks.text: On the contrary, Russia's public health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, said that two commissions investigating biosafety procedures at the institute found "no evidence of an accident involving pathogenic microorganisms." The Russian news agency TASS, citing Rospotrebnadzor, also reported that tests on the deceased employee detected no microorganisms linked to her professional activity.

Some social media users have tried to debunk the claim about a broken test tube, pointing to safety standards in high-containment laboratories, where the use of glassware may be restricted or completely banned to reduce the risk of accidents.

The Irkutsk institute does work with highly pathogenic microorganisms, including strains classified in Russia's highest pathogenicity groups, such as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.

However, DW could not independently verify the formally designated biosafety level of the institute's laboratories. Biosafety level, or BSL, is an international classification describing the containment measures required when handling dangerous pathogens, with BSL-4 reserved for the most hazardous agents.
DW asked the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute to comment on the alleged incident and its laboratory safety procedures but had received no response by the time of publication.
WHO website update unrelated to the Russian case

Claim: "The WHO appears to have updated its fact sheet on plague the same day the Irkutsk lab worker presented at hospital, with (probably) the plague." This claim appeared in a number of posts on X, each reaching thousands of users.
DW Fact check: Misleading
The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its plague fact sheet on the same day the Russian laboratory worker was hospitalized, but no evidence links the two events.

blocks.caption: Many social media users have linked the WHO’s recent update of its plague fact sheet to the alleged case in IrkutskImage: x.com

blocks.text: According to media reports, the laboratory worker may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis around September 25. Four days later, on September 29, she was hospitalized in Shelekhov with severe respiratory symptoms.

The WHO updated its plague fact sheet on September 29, the same day it published a news release on global trends in cholera, meningitis and plague. The update was part of a broader WHO publication cycle on infectious disease.

The release reported global surveillance data covering 2019 to 2025 and said the findings were published in the latest edition of the Weekly Epidemiological Record, which was released on September 25.
The timing therefore appears coincidental. The previous version of the WHO's plague fact sheet, accessible as an archived page, was dated July 7, 2022.

The social media account sharing the claim also changed its name in October to one that suggests it is reporting live from Irkutsk. Its profile describes itself as providing "sourced updates on the Irkutsk lab leak" and "latest news as it breaks live." However, the account's profile indicates that it was created in May and is based in Australia.
Such accounts can emerge quickly during breaking news events, presenting themselves as local or specialist sources while sharing unverified information.
Old video falsely linked to current plague claims in Russia

Claim: As news of the plague spreads, some old videos are being repurposed, adding to the disinformation. In one such video posted on X, a user claimed that the plague has also spread to other parts of Russia. The caption in Russian reads, "The plague marches across Russia. God has heard our prayers!"

The video is old and unrelated to the current developments in Irkutsk. A reverse image search reveals that the video was initially posted on August 31 this year, claiming that it showed the Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, a tourist destination around 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miiles)from Irkutsk.

blocks.caption: The video shared by users does show a region in Russia where the plague pathogen has been detected, but it is thousands of kilometres from IrkutskImage: x.com

blocks.text: The old video has been viewed more than 1.7 million times on Instagram. The same video was also posted on Telegram. The Russian news agency TASS reported on August 31 that the plague pathogen had been detected in local squirrels and that the area had been closed to tourists.

In the video, a person can be heard saying, "It's at the turnoff from the paved road toward Serebryany Istochnik" in Russian. Serebryany Istochnik, or Silver Spring, is a spring located in the Dzhily-Su area in Kabardino-Balkaria.

The situation in the Irkutsk region is still being investigated, but there are no confirmed reports of a plague outbreak in Russia. Health authorities have introduced precautionary measures following the death of the laboratory worker, while tests are reportedly being carried out.
